ecg-tachy-001.question: A 74-year-old man has had palpitations since yesterday. What is the diagnosis on this tracing (lead II)?
commentaires: Correct: irregularly irregular RR intervals, no organised P waves and a fibrillating baseline (f waves).
Incorrect: flutter, even with variable conduction, shows organised sawtooth F waves, which are absent here.
Incorrect: AVNRT is a perfectly regular tachycardia.
Incorrect: bigeminy alternates short and long cycles, with visible premature P waves.
ecg-tachy-001.explication: On this tracing the ventricular rhythm is completely irregular (with no periodicity), the QRS complexes are narrow and no organised P wave is visible, the baseline showing fine fibrillatory activity: this is atrial fibrillation. Atrial activity consists only of chaotic f waves, sometimes barely visible and often best seen in V1. Flutter, even with variable conduction, retains organised sawtooth F waves at ~300/min, which makes it recognisable despite the irregular QRS complexes. AVNRT is a regular tachycardia. Atrial bigeminy is "regularly irregular" (alternating short and long cycles) with visible premature P waves.
ecg-tachy-001.aRetenir: Irregularly irregular rhythm + no organised P waves = AF until proven otherwise.
ecg-tachy-001.rappel: An irregular narrow-QRS tachycardia has three main differential diagnoses: AF, atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia with variable conduction, and multifocal atrial tachycardia (or frequent PACs). The approach is to look for organised atrial activity: regular sawtooth F waves (flutter), distinct P waves separated by an isoelectric baseline (atrial tachycardia, with ≥ 3 morphologies in multifocal atrial tachycardia), or chaotic f waves of varying rate and amplitude (AF). At fast rates, AF may look regular: measure the RR intervals with callipers on a long rhythm strip. Tremor or artefact can mimic f waves.

ecg-tachy-002.question: According to the 2024 ESC guidelines, what is the minimum recording duration required to diagnose clinical AF on a single-lead tracing (patch, validated smartwatch, Holter)?
commentaires: Incorrect: 10 s is the length of a standard 12-lead ECG, which is sufficient on its own, but it is not the threshold for single-lead tracings.
Correct: a tracing of at least 30 s showing an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves, reviewed by a physician.
Incorrect: 6 minutes is the threshold used for device-detected atrial high-rate episodes (AHRE).
Incorrect: no 24-hour duration is required; that is the length of a standard Holter recording.
ecg-tachy-002.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines accept a diagnosis of clinical AF on a standard 12-lead ECG, or on a single- or multi-lead tracing of at least 30 seconds showing an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves. The 30 s threshold is the one historically used to define an AF episode. The 6-minute duration refers to device-detected atrial high-rate episodes (AHRE/subclinical AF), which is an entirely different concept. A 10 s tracing corresponds to the standard 12-lead ECG, which is sufficient on its own, but this is not the threshold for single-lead recordings. The tracing must be reviewed by a physician: the wearable device's algorithm is not enough.
ecg-tachy-002.aRetenir: Clinical AF = 12-lead ECG or a tracing ≥ 30 s interpreted by a physician.
ecg-tachy-002.rappel: The 2024 ESC guidelines classify AF by duration and management: first-diagnosed, paroxysmal (terminating spontaneously or with cardioversion within 7 days), persistent (beyond 7 days), long-standing persistent (more than 12 months when rhythm control is being considered) and permanent (a shared decision to make no further attempt to restore sinus rhythm). Atrial high-rate episodes detected by a pacemaker, ICD or implantable loop recorder (device-detected subclinical AF) are not clinical AF: they must be checked on the stored EGM, and their thromboembolic risk is lower than that of clinical AF.

ecg-tachy-003.question: A patient in permanent AF is taking digoxin. The ECG now shows a perfectly regular rhythm at 42 bpm with narrow QRS complexes and no visible P waves. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Spontaneous return to slow sinus rhythm
Good rate control, no action needed
Complete AV block with junctional escape
commentaires: Incorrect: 8:1 conduction is exceptional and organised F waves would be visible.
Incorrect: a return to sinus rhythm would require visible P waves before each QRS.
Incorrect: this is the classic trap; digoxin and potassium levels should be checked and the patient monitored.
Correct: AF that becomes regular and slow suggests complete AV block with a narrow escape rhythm, related to digoxin.
ecg-tachy-003.explication: In AF the ventricular response is inherently irregular. "Regularisation" of the ventricular rhythm, especially at a slow rate, should raise the suspicion of complete AV block with an escape rhythm (junctional if the QRS is narrow, ventricular if it is wide). On digoxin, digitalis toxicity must also be suspected (it can also cause a regularised accelerated junctional rhythm). A return to sinus rhythm would require visible P waves. 8:1 flutter is exceptional and would still show F waves. Regarding this tracing as "good rate control" is the classic trap: digoxin and potassium levels should be measured and the patient monitored.
ecg-tachy-003.aRetenir: AF that becomes regular and slow = complete AV block (and digitalis toxicity) until proven otherwise.
ecg-tachy-003.rappel: Digoxin slows AV nodal conduction through a vagal effect and increases automaticity and triggered activity (delayed afterdepolarisations) through calcium overload. The "scooped" ST segment reflects digoxin effect, not toxicity. ECG signs of toxicity combine increased excitability with depressed conduction: bigeminal PVCs, accelerated junctional rhythm, atrial tachycardia with block, AV block of any degree and, more specifically, bidirectional VT. Hypokalaemia, renal impairment and some interactions (amiodarone, verapamil) favour toxicity. Management consists of stopping digoxin, correcting potassium and, in severe cases, digoxin-specific Fab fragments.

ecg-tachy-004.question: Which of the following are part of the ECG definition of atrial fibrillation?
commentaires: Correct: irregularly irregular RR intervals when AV conduction is not impaired.
Correct: no organised P waves; atrial activity consists only of f waves.
Incorrect: without P waves there is no PR interval; a constant PR indicates an organised atrial rhythm.
Incorrect: rate is not part of the definition; AF can be slow.
ecg-tachy-004.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines define AF on the ECG as irregularly irregular RR intervals (when AV conduction is not impaired), the absence of distinct, repeating P waves and irregular atrial activity. The f waves, sometimes coarse and sometimes almost invisible, are best seen in V1. Without P waves there can be no PR interval: a constant PR indicates, on the contrary, an organised atrial rhythm. Ventricular rate is not part of the definition: AF can be slow (elderly patients, rate-slowing drugs, AV nodal disease). A regular rhythm in AF should raise the suspicion of complete AV block, flutter or atrial tachycardia.
ecg-tachy-004.aRetenir: AF: irregularly irregular RR intervals, no organised P waves, f waves.
ecg-tachy-004.rappel: In AF, atrial activity is disorganised, with rapid f waves (typically 350–600 per minute) of varying amplitude and morphology: coarse or almost invisible. The ventricular rate does not depend on the atrium but on the AV nodal filter: AV nodal refractory period, autonomic tone, rate-slowing drugs and concealed penetration of atrial impulses into the node. This is what makes the ventricular response irregular, and explains why it can be slow without AV block. A very fast response with wide and varying QRS complexes should raise the suspicion of pre-excitation.

ecg-tachy-005.question: A 67-year-old man has had palpitations and breathlessness for two days. Which diagnosis should you consider first on this tracing (lead II)?
commentaires: Correct: regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at around 150 bpm with two atrial deflections per QRS: 2:1 flutter.
Incorrect: one P wave per QRS and a gradual onset; here there are two atrial deflections per cycle.
Incorrect: in AVNRT the retrograde P wave is buried in the QRS; two atrial waves per cycle are not seen.
Incorrect: it keeps an isoelectric baseline between distinct P waves; here atrial activity is continuous.
ecg-tachy-005.explication: On this tracing the tachycardia is regular with narrow QRS complexes at around 150 bpm, with one atrial wave in the T wave and another just before each QRS. A regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at about 150 bpm should always prompt a search for 2:1 atrial flutter (300/2). One F wave is often hidden in the QRS or T wave, creating the illusion of sinus rhythm or SVT. The presence of two atrial deflections per QRS is the decisive clue. Sinus tachycardia starts and ends gradually, with a single P wave per QRS; focal atrial tachycardia keeps an isoelectric baseline between distinct P waves. When in doubt, vagal manoeuvres or adenosine unmask the F waves by transiently slowing AV conduction without terminating the flutter.
ecg-tachy-005.aRetenir: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 150 bpm: think of 2:1 flutter.
ecg-tachy-005.rappel: In a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia, the response to vagal manoeuvres or adenosine (rapid bolus, with a recorded ECG) is diagnostic. Abrupt termination points to a tachycardia that uses the AV node (AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT). Transient ventricular slowing unmasking persistent atrial activity indicates atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia. Gradual slowing followed by re-acceleration suggests sinus tachycardia or an automatic atrial tachycardia. To look for hidden F waves, examine the inferior leads and V1 and search for an atrial deflection midway between two QRS complexes.

ecg-tachy-006.question: In typical counterclockwise flutter (cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent), what is the usual appearance of the F waves?
options: Positive in II, III, aVF and negative in V1
Visible only on an oesophageal lead
Positive and peaked in all leads
Negative in II, III, aVF and positive in V1
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the pattern of typical clockwise flutter, which travels round the same circuit in the opposite direction.
Incorrect: F waves are clearly visible on the surface ECG, particularly in the inferior leads and V1.
Incorrect: F-wave polarity differs between the inferior leads and V1.
Correct: negative sawtooth F waves in the inferior leads and positive in V1 (ascending septal activation).
ecg-tachy-006.explication: In typical counterclockwise flutter, activation travels down the RA lateral wall, crosses the cavotricuspid isthmus and then ascends the septum. The result is negative sawtooth F waves with no isoelectric baseline in the inferior leads, and positive F waves in V1. This is the most common form (about 90% of typical flutters). The clockwise form, which travels in the opposite direction round the same circuit, produces F waves that are positive in the inferior leads and negative in V1. The circuit is the same in both cases: cavotricuspid isthmus ablation treats both.
ecg-tachy-006.aRetenir: Typical counterclockwise flutter: F waves negative in the inferior leads, positive in V1.
ecg-tachy-006.rappel: Typical atrial flutter is a right atrial macro-re-entry around the tricuspid annulus, with the cavotricuspid isthmus (between the tricuspid annulus and the inferior vena cava) as its obligatory pathway. The crista terminalis and the vena cava form the posterior barrier of the circuit. Electrophysiological proof of isthmus dependence is concealed entrainment from the isthmus with a post-pacing interval close to the tachycardia cycle length. Ablation aims at bidirectional conduction block across the isthmus; according to the 2019 ESC guidelines, it is recommended (class I) for symptomatic, recurrent CTI-dependent flutter.

ecg-tachy-007.question: In typical clockwise flutter, F waves are usually positive in the inferior leads and negative in V1.
commentaires: Correct: same circuit as counterclockwise flutter but travelled in the opposite direction, hence F waves positive in the inferior leads and negative in V1.
Incorrect: the statement is true; only F-wave polarity changes, the cavotricuspid circuit remaining the same.
ecg-tachy-007.explication: Clockwise flutter uses the same circuit as counterclockwise flutter (round the tricuspid annulus, through the cavotricuspid isthmus), but in the opposite direction. Septal activation becomes descending and lateral wall activation ascending, which reverses F-wave polarity: positive (often broad and notched) in II, III and aVF and negative in V1. It is still "typical" in the anatomical sense because it is cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent. It should therefore not be mistaken for atypical left atrial flutter on the ECG appearance alone. Definitive proof of the circuit relies on the electrophysiological study (entrainment, mapping).
ecg-tachy-007.aRetenir: Clockwise or counterclockwise, typical flutter is cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent; only F-wave polarity changes.
ecg-tachy-007.rappel: The ESC/NASPE classification (Saoudi, 2001) is based on mechanism and anatomy, not on ECG appearance. "Typical" flutter refers to any right atrial macro-re-entry dependent on the cavotricuspid isthmus, whether it rotates counterclockwise or clockwise. "Atypical" flutters are macro-re-entries that do not use the isthmus: circuits around right atrial scars (atriotomy), perimitral circuits, roof-dependent circuits or circuits around the left pulmonary veins. F-wave polarity suggests the circuit but does not prove it; only entrainment and mapping demonstrate it.

ecg-tachy-008.question: Atrial flutter with an atrial rate of 300/min and fixed 4:1 AV conduction. What ventricular rate would you expect? And with 2:1 conduction?
ecg-tachy-008.reponseAttendue: 75 bpm with 4:1 conduction (300/4); 150 bpm with 2:1 conduction (300/2).
ecg-tachy-008.explication: The ventricular rate in flutter is calculated by dividing the atrial rate by the conduction ratio. Untreated typical flutter runs at around 250–350/min (in practice ~300/min). With 4:1 conduction this gives 75 bpm, with 3:1 100 bpm and with 2:1 150 bpm. On a class IC antiarrhythmic drug or amiodarone, the atrial rate may slow (200–250/min), which paradoxically exposes the patient to the risk of 1:1 conduction with very fast ventricular rates.
ecg-tachy-008.aRetenir: Ventricular rate in flutter = atrial rate / conduction ratio.
ecg-tachy-008.rappel: In atrial flutter, the AV node filters the rapid atrial activity: even ratios (2:1, 4:1) are the most common, odd ratios rarer. Fixed conduction produces a regular ventricular rhythm; variable conduction, often due to Wenckebach behaviour within the AV node, produces an irregular but "grouped" rhythm, with RR intervals that are multiples of the atrial cycle, unlike AF. The conduction ratio depends on autonomic tone and rate-slowing drugs; 1:1 conduction may occur during exercise, under catecholamines, or when the flutter cycle is slowed by an antiarrhythmic drug.

ecg-tachy-009.question: A patient on flecainide for paroxysmal AF presents with poorly tolerated palpitations. ECG: regular wide-QRS tachycardia at 230 bpm. What diagnosis should you consider and what is the mechanism? What preventive measure should have been combined with the treatment?
ecg-tachy-009.reponseAttendue: Atrial flutter ("class IC flutter") slowed by flecainide (~230/min) and conducted 1:1, with QRS widening due to the use-dependent effect of the sodium channel blocker. Prevention: combine an AV nodal blocking agent (beta-blocker or rate-limiting calcium channel blocker) with the class IC drug.
ecg-tachy-009.explication: Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs can convert AF into atrial flutter, whose rate they slow (often to 200–250/min). The AV node, able to conduct at that rate, then lets the flutter through 1:1. The use-dependent effect of sodium channel blockade widens the QRS at fast rates, so the tracing mimics VT. This is why the ESC recommends combining an AV nodal blocking agent (beta-blocker, verapamil or diltiazem) with flecainide or propafenone. Acutely, such a poorly tolerated presentation calls for synchronised external cardioversion.
ecg-tachy-009.aRetenir: Class IC drug without an AV nodal blocker = risk of 1:1 flutter with wide QRS complexes.
ecg-tachy-009.rappel: Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone) block the fast sodium channel with slow unbinding kinetics: their effect increases with heart rate (use dependence), hence QRS widening at fast rates, particularly during exercise. They are contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease or significant LV dysfunction. In selected patients without structural heart disease, they can be used long term or as a "pill-in-the-pocket", always combined with an AV nodal blocking drug. Any QRS widening on a class IC drug should prompt a search for overdose or a tachycardia conducted 1:1.

ecg-tachy-010.question: A regular atrial tachycardia occurs after several AF ablations (pulmonary vein isolation and roof line). The atrial waves are clearly positive in V1. Which statement is correct?
options: The circuit is most probably the cavotricuspid isthmus
An isoelectric baseline between waves rules out macro-re-entry
A positive atrial wave in V1 points to a left-sided circuit
An atrial rate below 250/min rules out flutter
commentaires: Incorrect: after several AF ablations, circuits are frequently left-sided; the isthmus is not the most likely site.
Incorrect: in a scarred atrium, macro-re-entry can retain an isoelectric baseline (silent slow conduction).
Correct: after AF ablation, clearly positive atrial activity in V1 points to a left-sided circuit (perimitral, roof).
Incorrect: atrial rate is not a reliable criterion, especially on antiarrhythmic drugs.
ecg-tachy-010.explication: After AF ablation, atrial tachycardias are frequently left-sided: perimitral or roof-dependent macro-re-entry, or focal tachycardias/micro-re-entry through gaps in ablation lines. Clearly positive atrial activity in V1 favours a left-sided origin; it is not specific, however, since typical counterclockwise flutter is also positive in V1 (but with negative F waves in the inferior leads). In these patients with atrial scarring, an isoelectric baseline may be present despite macro-re-entry ("silent" slow conduction zones). Atrial rate is not a reliable criterion, especially on antiarrhythmic drugs. Accurate diagnosis of the circuit relies on electroanatomical mapping.
ecg-tachy-010.aRetenir: After AF ablation, the surface ECG gives clues but cannot establish the mechanism: mapping is essential.
ecg-tachy-010.rappel: Atrial tachycardias after AF ablation have three mechanisms: left atrial macro-re-entry (perimitral around the mitral annulus, roof-dependent around the pulmonary veins), localised re-entry or focal sources related to reconnections and gaps in ablation lines, and CTI-dependent flutter. Diagnosis relies on activation mapping, which should cover the whole cycle in a macro-re-entry, and on entrainment from several sites. A left atrial macro-re-entry is treated by an ablation line interrupting the circuit (mitral isthmus, roof), whose conduction block must be verified.

ecg-tachy-011.question: Which of the following favour focal atrial tachycardia rather than flutter (macro-re-entry)?
options: P waves separated by a clear isoelectric baseline
Gradual acceleration at onset ("warm-up") then slowing before termination
Continuous undulating atrial activity with no return to baseline
commentaires: Correct: centrifugal activation from a focus leaves an isoelectric baseline between P waves.
Correct: "warm-up/cool-down" behaviour is typical of an automatic mechanism.
Incorrect: an atrial rate close to 300/min suggests typical flutter instead.
Incorrect: continuous undulating activity reflects macro-re-entry (flutter).
ecg-tachy-011.explication: Focal atrial tachycardia arises from a focus (automaticity, triggered activity or micro-re-entry) and activates the atrium centrifugally. This leaves an isoelectric baseline between P waves, whose morphology differs from the sinus P wave. "Warm-up/cool-down" behaviour is typical of an automatic mechanism. Conversely, continuous undulating activity with no baseline reflects macro-re-entry (flutter), and an atrial rate close to 300/min suggests typical flutter instead, although rate alone is not decisive. Caution: these criteria are only indicative; macro-re-entry in a scarred atrium can show an isoelectric baseline, and a fast focal tachycardia can appear continuous.
ecg-tachy-011.aRetenir: An isoelectric baseline, a P wave different from sinus and warm-up favour focal atrial tachycardia.
ecg-tachy-011.rappel: Focal atrial tachycardias arise from a focus through abnormal automaticity, triggered activity or micro-re-entry. Their preferred sites follow anatomical structures: crista terminalis, tricuspid and mitral annuli, coronary sinus ostium, para-Hisian region, atrial appendages and pulmonary veins. The atrial cycle length is usually longer than in flutter, although rate alone cannot settle the question. Adenosine can terminate some focal atrial tachycardias (particularly those due to triggered activity), so termination does not exclude an atrial mechanism. Ablation of the focus is the reference treatment for recurrent forms.

ecg-tachy-012.question: Focal atrial tachycardia: P wave positive in V1, negative in I and aVL, clearly positive in II, III and aVF. What is the most likely origin?
commentaires: Incorrect: a right pulmonary vein origin also gives a positive P wave in V1, but positive in I and aVL.
Incorrect: the coronary sinus ostium gives negative P waves in the inferior leads.
Incorrect: a tricuspid origin gives negative P waves in V1.
Correct: P positive in V1 and negative in I/aVL = left lateral origin; positive inferior leads = superior origin.
ecg-tachy-012.explication: According to the Kistler algorithm, a P wave that is positive in V1 and negative (or isoelectric) in I/aVL points to a left lateral atrial origin, typically the left pulmonary veins. Clearly positive inferior leads indicate a superior origin (superior vein). An origin in the right pulmonary veins also produces a positive P wave in V1, but positive in I and aVL. The coronary sinus ostium produces negative P waves in the inferior leads. The tricuspid annulus produces negative P waves in V1. These rules remain approximate and must be confirmed by mapping.
ecg-tachy-012.aRetenir: P positive in V1 and negative in I/aVL = left lateral origin (left pulmonary veins); positive inferior leads = superior origin.
ecg-tachy-012.rappel: The Kistler algorithm localises focal atrial tachycardia from P-wave morphology. Lead V1 first separates right lateral origins (crista terminalis, tricuspid annulus: negative or biphasic negative–positive P wave in V1) from left-sided or septal origins (positive P wave in V1). The inferior leads indicate height: positive for a superior origin (superior veins, appendages, high crista), negative for an inferior origin (coronary sinus ostium, inferior annulus). Leads I and aVL, negative or isoelectric for a left lateral origin, distinguish the left from the right pulmonary veins. The crista terminalis is the most common right-sided site.

ecg-tachy-013.question: A patient with COPD presents with an acute respiratory exacerbation. Irregular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 120 bpm; each QRS is preceded by a P wave, but at least 3 different P-wave morphologies and variable PR intervals are identified. What is the diagnosis and what is the principle of treatment?
ecg-tachy-013.reponseAttendue: Multifocal atrial tachycardia. Treatment: correct the cause (respiratory decompensation, hypoxia, hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia, theophylline…); rate-control drugs (non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, possibly a cardioselective beta-blocker) if needed; electrical cardioversion is ineffective.
ecg-tachy-013.explication: Multifocal atrial tachycardia combines a rate > 100 bpm, at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and variable PP, PR and RR intervals. It is typically associated with decompensated chronic lung disease, hypoxia and metabolic disturbances. It is often mistaken for AF because of its irregularity, but the P waves are clearly distinct, with an isoelectric baseline. Treatment is first and foremost that of the underlying cause; electrical cardioversion and ablation have no first-line role.
ecg-tachy-013.aRetenir: Irregular tachycardia with ≥ 3 P-wave morphologies in a patient with respiratory failure = multifocal atrial tachycardia: treat the cause.
ecg-tachy-013.rappel: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is probably due to triggered activity in several atrial foci, favoured by hypoxia, acidosis, atrial stretch, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and sympathomimetic drugs (beta-2 agonists, theophylline). Defined by at least three P-wave morphologies and a rate > 100 bpm, it is distinguished from multifocal atrial rhythm ("wandering atrial pacemaker"), whose rate is < 100 bpm. It responds poorly to electrical cardioversion and antiarrhythmic drugs. Alongside treatment of the cause, intravenous magnesium and rate-slowing drugs (verapamil, diltiazem, a cardioselective beta-blocker if respiratory function allows) may help.

ecg-tachy-014.question: A 28-year-old woman reports palpitations of abrupt onset and offset. This tracing was recorded during an episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?
commentaires: Correct: regular narrow-QRS tachycardia, abrupt onset and offset, no visible P waves: AVNRT first and foremost.
Incorrect: the QRS complexes are narrow, without an RBBB-like pattern; the context suggests a junctional tachycardia.
Incorrect: the rhythm is perfectly regular.
Incorrect: abrupt onset and offset and no visible P waves before the QRS: this is not a sinus rhythm.
ecg-tachy-014.explication: On this tracing the tachycardia is regular with narrow QRS complexes at around 180 bpm and no visible P waves (retrograde P wave buried in the QRS). In a young woman with abrupt onset and offset, this picture first suggests AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT), the most common junctional tachycardia. AF is irregular. Sinus tachycardia, even when inappropriate, has a gradual onset and offset and visible P waves before each QRS. Fascicular VT has relatively narrow QRS complexes (often 120–140 ms) but with an RBBB-like pattern, which is not the case here. The main differential diagnosis remains orthodromic AVRT via an accessory pathway (concealed or manifest).
ecg-tachy-014.aRetenir: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia with abrupt onset/offset and no visible P waves: AVNRT first and foremost.
ecg-tachy-014.rappel: AVNRT relies on dual AV nodal physiology: a slow pathway (short refractory period) and a fast pathway (long refractory period). In the typical slow–fast form, a PAC blocked in the fast pathway conducts down the slow pathway and back up the fast pathway; atria and ventricles are activated almost simultaneously. The retrograde P wave is therefore buried in the QRS or seen just after it (pseudo-r' in V1, pseudo-S in the inferior leads), with an RP interval < 70 ms. A longer RP interval points to orthodromic AVRT. Atypical (fast–slow) AVNRT produces a long RP interval with negative P waves in the inferior leads.

ecg-tachy-015.question: Which ECG sign, absent in sinus rhythm and visible during tachycardia, is most suggestive of typical (slow–fast) AVNRT?
options: A delta wave appearing during tachycardia
Retrograde P wave in the ST segment, > 90 ms after the QRS
Pseudo-r' in V1 and pseudo-S in the inferior leads
commentaires: Incorrect: a delta wave is a sign of pre-excitation in sinus rhythm, not of AVNRT.
Incorrect: a long RP of this kind rather points to orthodromic AVRT.
Incorrect: electrical alternans is mainly related to the fast rate and is not specific.
Correct: the retrograde P wave emerges at the end of the QRS, creating a pseudo-r' in V1 and a pseudo-S in the inferior leads.
ecg-tachy-015.explication: In typical AVNRT, atrial activation (retrograde, via the fast pathway) and ventricular activation are almost simultaneous: the retrograde P wave is therefore hidden in the QRS or emerges at its end. It produces a pseudo-r' in V1 and a pseudo-S in the inferior leads, to be compared with the sinus rhythm tracing. The RP interval is very short (typically < 70 ms). A retrograde P wave clearly separated from the QRS (RP > 70–90 ms) rather points to orthodromic AVRT. A delta wave is a sign of pre-excitation in sinus rhythm. Electrical alternans is more common in AVRT but is mainly related to the fast rate and is not specific.
ecg-tachy-015.aRetenir: Typical AVNRT: retrograde P wave "within" the end of the QRS = pseudo-r' in V1, pseudo-S in the inferior leads.
ecg-tachy-015.rappel: Typical AVNRT usually starts with a PAC that blocks in the fast pathway and conducts over the slow pathway, with a sudden prolongation of the PR interval (slow-pathway "jump"). The circuit lies within the nodal region: neither the atria nor the ventricles are essential parts of it. A 2:1 AV block during tachycardia (most often infra-Hisian) is therefore compatible with AVNRT, whereas it excludes AVRT, which requires both chambers. Careful lead-by-lead comparison with the ECG in sinus rhythm remains the simplest tool for spotting a retrograde P wave fused with the end of the QRS.

ecg-tachy-016.question: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia at 200 bpm. A retrograde P wave (negative in the inferior leads) is seen in the ST segment, about 120 ms after QRS onset; RP < PR. What is the most likely mechanism?
commentaires: Incorrect: in typical AVNRT the RP is very short (< 70 ms), the P wave being buried in the QRS.
Incorrect: atypical AVNRT produces a long-RP tachycardia (RP > PR).
Correct: short RP but > 70 ms, retrograde P wave in the ST segment: retrograde conduction via the accessory pathway after the ventricles.
Incorrect: sinus tachycardia would show P waves positive in the inferior leads preceding the QRS.
ecg-tachy-016.explication: A short-RP tachycardia (RP < PR) with an RP > 70 ms is typical of orthodromic AVRT: the impulse travels down the AV node, activates the ventricles and then returns to the atria via the accessory pathway, which takes some time. In typical AVNRT the RP is much shorter (< 70 ms), the P wave being buried in the QRS. Atypical fast–slow AVNRT produces a long-RP tachycardia (RP > PR). Sinus tachycardia would show P waves positive in the inferior leads preceding the QRS. A definitive diagnosis remains electrophysiological.
ecg-tachy-016.aRetenir: Short RP but > 70 ms with a retrograde P wave in the ST segment: orthodromic AVRT.
ecg-tachy-016.rappel: Orthodromic AVRT is a macro-re-entry conducting down the AV node and His–Purkinje system and back up an accessory pathway; atria and ventricles are both part of the circuit, so the AV relationship is necessarily 1:1. Many pathways conduct only retrogradely: they are "concealed", with no pre-excitation in sinus rhythm, but can still sustain orthodromic AVRT. As a typical accessory pathway conducts non-decrementally, the RP interval stays fixed whatever the rate. The morphology of the retrograde P wave depends on the atrial insertion of the pathway (negative in lead I for a left lateral pathway).

ecg-tachy-017.question: Regular narrow-QRS long-RP tachycardia (RP > PR). Which diagnoses should be considered?
options: Orthodromic AVRT via a rapidly conducting accessory pathway
commentaires: Correct: the atrial P wave "conducts" to the next QRS, hence a long RP.
Correct: anterograde conduction via the fast pathway and slow retrograde conduction via the slow pathway: long RP.
Correct: posteroseptal accessory pathway with slow, decremental retrograde conduction; often incessant.
Incorrect: typical AVNRT is the archetypal very short-RP tachycardia.
Incorrect: a rapidly conducting accessory pathway produces a short-RP AVRT (> 70 ms), not a long RP.
ecg-tachy-017.explication: A long-RP tachycardia means that the P wave is closer to the next QRS than to the previous one. The three main diagnoses are atrial tachycardia (the P wave "conducts" to the next QRS), atypical fast–slow AVNRT (anterograde conduction via the fast pathway, slow retrograde conduction via the slow pathway) and permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia (PJRT, or Coumel tachycardia), which uses a posteroseptal accessory pathway with slow, decremental retrograde conduction. The latter, often incessant, can cause an arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy. Typical AVNRT, by contrast, is the archetypal very short-RP tachycardia, and orthodromic AVRT via a classic (rapidly conducting) accessory pathway produces a short RP, greater than 70 ms.
ecg-tachy-017.aRetenir: Long RP: atrial tachycardia, atypical AVNRT or PJRT (Coumel).
ecg-tachy-017.rappel: Permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia (PJRT, Coumel) is an orthodromic AVRT using a concealed accessory pathway with slow, decremental retrograde conduction, most often posteroseptal near the coronary sinus ostium. It produces deeply negative retrograde P waves in II, III and aVF with a long RP interval, restarts spontaneously without a premature beat, and often occurs in children or young adults. Its incessant nature exposes to tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, which is usually reversible after ablation. Atypical AVNRT has a similar ECG appearance: the distinction is made at EP study.

ecg-tachy-018.question: Termination of a regular narrow-QRS tachycardia with IV adenosine rules out atrial tachycardia.
commentaires: Incorrect: some focal atrial tachycardias (perinodal, triggered activity) are also terminated by adenosine.
Correct: it is the way the tachycardia terminates (on a P wave or on a QRS) that is informative, not termination itself.
ecg-tachy-018.explication: Adenosine terminates junctional tachycardias that use the AV node as part of their circuit (AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT), but some focal atrial tachycardias, particularly adenosine-sensitive ones (perinodal, triggered activity), are also terminated. Termination with adenosine therefore does not rule out atrial tachycardia. The way the tachycardia terminates is more informative: termination on a P wave (block in the AV node) argues against atrial tachycardia, since the atrial tachycardia would have to stop at the precise moment of AV block. When adenosine causes transient AV block with persisting atrial activity, an atrial tachycardia or flutter is unmasked. The ECG must always be recorded during the injection.
ecg-tachy-018.aRetenir: It is not termination with adenosine but the way the tachycardia terminates (or fails to) that guides the diagnosis.
ecg-tachy-018.rappel: Adenosine acts on A1 receptors: it transiently slows or blocks AV nodal conduction and shortens atrial refractoriness. Its half-life is a few seconds: it is given as a rapid bolus into a proximal vein, followed by a saline flush, in increasing doses (6 then 12 mg, or even 18 mg). Adverse effects are brief but alarming: flushing, chest tightness, pauses, bronchospasm. It can trigger AF, which is dangerous in the presence of pre-excitation. Its effect is enhanced by dipyridamole, in heart transplant recipients or via a central line, and reduced by theophylline and caffeine.

ecg-tachy-019.question: During orthodromic AVRT, the development of functional left bundle branch block prolongs the VA interval and the tachycardia cycle length by about 40 ms. What can be concluded?
options: Right-sided accessory pathway, contralateral to the block
Left-sided accessory pathway, ipsilateral to the block
AVNRT: bundle branch block does not affect this circuit
commentaires: Incorrect: a block contralateral to the pathway does not alter the circuit; it is RBBB that slows AVRT via a right-sided pathway.
Correct: Coumel's law; the detour through the contralateral ventricle prolongs the VA, proving that a left-sided pathway is part of the circuit.
Incorrect: in AVNRT, bundle branch block does not alter the cycle length, whereas here the cycle length increases.
Incorrect: in atrial tachycardia, aberrancy does not alter the tachycardia cycle length.
ecg-tachy-019.explication: This is Coumel's law: when functional bundle branch block occurs on the same side as the accessory pathway, the activation wavefront must detour through the contralateral ventricle before reaching the pathway. The circuit lengthens, increasing the VA interval and the tachycardia cycle length (VA prolongation of around 35 ms or more for a lateral pathway). This phenomenon proves both the presence of an accessory pathway participating in the circuit and its laterality. In AVNRT or atrial tachycardia, bundle branch block does not alter the cycle length. Conversely, right bundle branch block that slows the tachycardia points to a right-sided pathway.
ecg-tachy-019.aRetenir: Cycle length prolongation with functional bundle branch block = accessory pathway ipsilateral to the block (Coumel's law).
ecg-tachy-019.rappel: Aberrant conduction is a functional bundle branch block: an early supraventricular impulse reaches a bundle branch that is still refractory (phase 3). It is favoured by a long–short cycle sequence (Ashman phenomenon), more often affects the right bundle branch, whose refractory period is longer, and can be perpetuated by concealed retrograde conduction into the blocked branch ("linking"). During AVRT, only a block ipsilateral to a free-wall pathway clearly prolongs the VA interval; with a septal pathway the prolongation is small, which limits the localising value of the sign.

ecg-tachy-020.question: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia. Which findings favour orthodromic AVRT over typical AVNRT?
options: Retrograde P wave visible in the ST segment with an RP > 70 ms
Slowing of the tachycardia when functional bundle branch block develops
Electrical alternans of the QRS, a specific sign of AVRT
Pseudo-r' wave in V1 during tachycardia, absent in sinus rhythm
commentaires: Correct: retrograde conduction via the accessory pathway after the ventricles separates the retrograde P wave from the QRS.
Correct: Coumel's law; block ipsilateral to the pathway lengthens the circuit and proves accessory pathway participation.
Incorrect: more common in AVRT, it depends mainly on rate and is not specific.
Incorrect: a pseudo-r' reflects a retrograde P wave fused with the QRS, typical of AVNRT.
ecg-tachy-020.explication: In orthodromic AVRT, retrograde atrial activation travels via the accessory pathway after ventricular activation: the retrograde P wave is separated from the QRS (RP > 70 ms) and often visible in the ST segment. Cycle length prolongation with functional bundle branch block ipsilateral to the pathway (Coumel's law) proves accessory pathway participation. Pre-excitation in sinus rhythm also makes AVRT very likely, although AVNRT may coexist. A pseudo-r' in V1, by contrast, reflects a retrograde P wave fused with the QRS and is typical of AVNRT. Electrical alternans, more common in AVRT, is mainly related to the fast rate: it is not specific.
ecg-tachy-020.aRetenir: RP > 70 ms, Coumel's law and pre-excitation in sinus rhythm favour AVRT.
ecg-tachy-020.rappel: The retrograde atrial activation sequence helps identify the mechanism of a narrow-QRS tachycardia. In AVNRT and with septal pathways, activation is concentric, starting at the septum, with retrograde P waves that are negative in the inferior leads and roughly symmetrical. A free-wall pathway produces eccentric activation: P wave negative in lead I for a left-sided pathway, positive in lead I for a right-sided one. ST depression is common during tachycardia and indicates neither the mechanism nor coronary ischaemia. Definitive diagnosis relies on the EP study.

ecg-tachy-021.question: Resting ECG of a 15-year-old boy being investigated for palpitations. What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
commentaires: Correct: short PR, slurred initial QRS upstroke (delta wave) and wide QRS: pre-excitation via an accessory pathway.
Incorrect: the PR is in fact short (< 120 ms).
Incorrect: bundle branch block widens the QRS without shortening the PR or creating a delta wave.
Incorrect: hyperkalaemia first causes peaked T waves and does not shorten the PR.
ecg-tachy-021.explication: On this tracing the PR is short, the QRS begins with a slurred upstroke (delta wave) and is widened. This triad of short PR (< 120 ms), delta wave and wide QRS reflects ventricular pre-excitation: part of the ventricle is activated early via an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node. The QRS is a fusion of activation via the accessory pathway and via the normal conduction system. Secondary repolarisation abnormalities are common and should not be mistaken for ischaemia. First-degree AV block prolongs the PR, bundle branch block does not shorten the PR, and hyperkalaemia first causes peaked T waves.
ecg-tachy-021.aRetenir: Short PR + delta wave + wide QRS = pre-excitation.
ecg-tachy-021.rappel: An accessory pathway is a muscle bundle crossing the AV annulus outside the AV node; it usually conducts without decrement. The degree of pre-excitation depends on AV nodal conduction time and on the distance between the pathway and the sinus node: a left lateral pathway, reached later, may produce subtle pre-excitation, whereas a right-sided pathway often produces obvious pre-excitation. Pre-excitation may be intermittent. A negative delta wave can mimic a pathological Q wave (pseudo-infarction pattern). Ebstein anomaly is associated with right-sided, sometimes multiple, pathways.

ecg-tachy-022.question: Wolff–Parkinson–White "syndrome" refers to ECG pre-excitation associated with symptomatic tachyarrhythmias; isolated asymptomatic pre-excitation is a WPW "pattern".
commentaires: Correct: pre-excitation + arrhythmia = syndrome; isolated pre-excitation = pattern, which is managed differently.
Incorrect: the statement is true; this distinction guides risk stratification in asymptomatic individuals.
ecg-tachy-022.explication: The terminology distinguishes the ECG pattern of pre-excitation (WPW pattern), often found incidentally, from WPW syndrome, which combines pre-excitation with arrhythmias (AVRT, pre-excited AF). This distinction has practical consequences: management of asymptomatic individuals relies on risk stratification (exercise test, Holter, or even an EP study), whereas symptomatic syndrome generally calls for ablation. The main risk, although rare, is sudden cardiac death from pre-excited AF degenerating into VF.
ecg-tachy-022.aRetenir: Pre-excitation + arrhythmia = WPW syndrome; pre-excitation alone = WPW pattern.
ecg-tachy-022.rappel: In an asymptomatic individual with pre-excitation, the aim is to identify a pathway capable of conducting AF very rapidly. Risk stratification starts with non-invasive tests (intermittent pre-excitation, abrupt loss during exercise); when no low-risk feature is found, an EP study with isoprenaline measures the pathway's anterograde refractory period, the shortest pre-excited RR interval during induced AF and the inducibility of AVRT, and looks for multiple pathways. The 2019 ESC guidelines recommend this study for people with high-risk occupations and competitive athletes, and ablation when high-risk features are found.

ecg-tachy-023.question: Pre-excitation with a delta wave negative in I and aVL, positive in II, III and aVF, and a dominant R wave from V1. Where is the accessory pathway probably located?
commentaires: Incorrect: a posteroseptal pathway produces a negative delta wave in III/aVF.
Incorrect: right-sided pathways produce an LBBB-like pattern with late transition, not a dominant R in V1.
Incorrect: an anteroseptal pathway produces a QS or rS pattern in V1.
Correct: the initial vector points away from I/aVL and anteriorly: negative delta in I/aVL, dominant R from V1.
ecg-tachy-023.explication: A left lateral pathway first activates the LV lateral wall, so the initial vector points away from I and aVL (negative delta wave) and anteriorly and rightward, producing a dominant R wave from V1. Right-sided pathways, by contrast, produce an LBBB-like pattern with a late transition (after V2–V3), because the right free wall is activated first. Anteroseptal pathways produce a delta wave positive in the inferior leads with QS/rS in V1, and posteroseptal pathways a delta wave negative in III/aVF. In practice, delta-wave polarity in V1 is the first step: positive (R > S) = left-sided pathway.
ecg-tachy-023.aRetenir: Negative delta in I/aVL and dominant R in V1: left lateral accessory pathway.
ecg-tachy-023.rappel: The initial vector of the pre-excited QRS points away from the ventricular insertion of the pathway: a negative delta wave identifies a lead "facing" the pathway. Delta-wave polarity is assessed over the first 20–40 ms, ideally during maximal pre-excitation (atrial pacing or adenosine), because fusion with nodal activation blunts the signs. Algorithms (Arruda in particular) work step by step: leads I and V1 separate left from right pathways, lead II identifies epicardial posteroseptal pathways, and aVF distinguishes anterior from posterior pathways. They guide the approach (transseptal, retro-aortic, coronary sinus); precise localisation relies on mapping.

ecg-tachy-024.question: Pre-excitation with a clearly negative delta wave in II (and in III, aVF). According to the Arruda algorithm, which location should be suspected?
commentaires: Correct: negative delta in II = subepicardial posteroseptal pathway, accessible via the coronary sinus (middle cardiac vein).
Incorrect: anteroseptal pathways produce a positive delta wave in the inferior leads.
Incorrect: left lateral pathways produce a negative delta wave in I/aVL, not in II.
Incorrect: Mahaim fibres, which are decremental, generally do not produce manifest pre-excitation in sinus rhythm.
ecg-tachy-024.explication: In the Arruda algorithm, a negative delta wave in II is the marker of a subepicardial posteroseptal pathway, accessible from the coronary sinus or its middle cardiac vein, and sometimes associated with a coronary sinus diverticulum. This information is of major practical value: it prepares the operator for mapping within the coronary sinus (prior angiography is useful) rather than simple endocardial ablation. Anteroseptal pathways produce a positive delta wave in the inferior leads. Left lateral pathways produce a negative delta wave in I/aVL. Mahaim fibres, which are decremental, generally do not produce manifest pre-excitation in sinus rhythm.
ecg-tachy-024.aRetenir: Negative delta in II = epicardial posteroseptal pathway (coronary sinus).
ecg-tachy-024.rappel: The posteroseptal (or inferior paraseptal) region is anatomically complex: pyramidal and close to the compact AV node, it contains the coronary sinus ostium and its branches (middle cardiac vein), sometimes a diverticulum. Pathways may insert epicardially, via the coronary sinus musculature, and escape right- or left-sided endocardial ablation. Ablation inside the coronary sinus is performed close to the coronary arteries (distal right coronary artery, circumflex artery): coronary angiography before energy delivery allows the distance to be checked. Atriofascicular (Mahaim) fibres, right-sided and decremental, produce an antidromic tachycardia with LBBB morphology.

ecg-tachy-025.question: A 32-year-old man with known pre-excitation has had palpitations for one hour and is haemodynamically stable. Here is the tracing. Which treatments are contraindicated?
options: IV flecainide in the absence of structural heart disease
Synchronised external cardioversion if haemodynamics deteriorate
commentaires: Correct: by slowing the AV node, they favour conduction over the accessory pathway and can precipitate VF.
Correct: digoxin slows the AV node and can shorten the accessory pathway refractory period.
Incorrect: flecainide slows conduction in the accessory pathway; it is an option in a stable patient.
Incorrect: synchronised cardioversion is the treatment of choice if the patient is unstable.
ecg-tachy-025.explication: The tracing shows a very fast irregular wide-QRS tachycardia: this is pre-excited AF, with atrial impulses conducting preferentially over the accessory pathway, hence wide, irregular QRS complexes of varying width (varying degrees of fusion). All AV nodal blocking agents (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin) are contraindicated because they favour conduction over the accessory pathway and can precipitate VF. The 2019 ESC guidelines also advise against IV amiodarone (class III). If the patient is unstable, synchronised external cardioversion is the treatment of choice; if stable, ibutilide or procainamide can be used (or flecainide, which slows accessory pathway conduction), followed by planned accessory pathway ablation.
ecg-tachy-025.aRetenir: Pre-excited AF: no AV nodal blocking agents (no adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers or digoxin); DC cardioversion if unstable.
ecg-tachy-025.rappel: During pre-excited AF, the ventricular rate depends on the anterograde refractory period of the accessory pathway, which lacks the filtering role of the AV node. Very fast, irregular, wide QRS complexes of varying morphology (varying fusion between pathway and node) are the clue. Blocking the AV node removes concealed retrograde penetration into the pathway and nodal competition, which accelerates conduction over the accessory pathway; digoxin also shortens its refractory period. After an episode of pre-excited AF, ablation of the accessory pathway is the definitive treatment, as the risk is degeneration into VF.

ecg-tachy-026.question: During pre-excited AF (spontaneous or induced), which shortest pre-excited RR interval (SPERRI) is classically regarded as a marker of an accessory pathway at high risk of sudden cardiac death?
commentaires: Incorrect: this threshold is too strict and would miss most high-risk pathways.
Correct: SPERRI ≤ 250 ms (rate ≥ 240 bpm) = high-risk accessory pathway (ESC 2019).
Incorrect: a 400 ms threshold would have no specificity.
Incorrect: 500 ms corresponds to 120 bpm, a rate with no prognostic value in pre-excited AF.
ecg-tachy-026.explication: The anterograde refractory period of the accessory pathway determines the maximum ventricular rate in pre-excited AF. A shortest RR interval between two pre-excited complexes ≤ 250 ms (i.e. a rate ≥ 240 bpm) is the classic marker of a high-risk pathway, with a risk of degeneration into VF. The 2019 ESC guidelines adopt this threshold, together with an anterograde effective refractory period ≤ 250 ms, inducible AVRT and multiple pathways, as high-risk criteria warranting ablation. A 400–500 ms threshold would have no specificity.
ecg-tachy-026.aRetenir: SPERRI ≤ 250 ms in AF = high-risk accessory pathway.
ecg-tachy-026.rappel: The anterograde refractory period of the accessory pathway sets the maximum ventricular rate it allows during AF: rate (bpm) = 60,000 / RR (ms). It shortens under catecholamines, which is why it should be assessed with isoprenaline during the EP study: a pathway that seems reassuring at rest may become dangerous during exercise. The mechanism of sudden cardiac death is AF conducted very rapidly to the ventricles, which degenerates into VF. The SPERRI is measured between two consecutive pre-excited complexes during spontaneous or induced AF.

ecg-tachy-027.question: In an asymptomatic individual with pre-excitation, abrupt and complete disappearance of the delta wave during an exercise test favours a low-risk accessory pathway.
commentaires: Correct: abrupt loss of the delta wave on exercise reflects a long anterograde refractory period of the pathway.
Incorrect: the statement is true; it is a gradual reduction of the delta wave that has no reassuring value.
ecg-tachy-027.explication: Abrupt, complete loss of pre-excitation as the sinus rate increases reflects block in the accessory pathway, and therefore a long anterograde refractory period: the pathway will not be able to conduct AF rapidly. This abrupt disappearance must be distinguished from a gradual reduction in pre-excitation, which merely reflects improved AV nodal conduction (more activation via the AV node) and is not reassuring. Intermittent pre-excitation on the ECG or Holter carries the same low-risk significance. These non-invasive criteria are proposed in the 2019 ESC guidelines for risk stratification of asymptomatic pre-excitation.
ecg-tachy-027.aRetenir: Abrupt loss of the delta wave on exercise = pathway with a long refractory period, low risk.
ecg-tachy-027.rappel: The pre-excited QRS is a fusion between activation over the accessory pathway and over the AV node: its appearance varies with AV nodal conduction. Sympathetic tone speeds up nodal conduction, which reduces the pre-excited component without saying anything about the pathway; only a sudden block in the pathway, observed in sinus rhythm, indicates a long refractory period. Intermittent pre-excitation on the ECG or Holter has the same meaning. These non-invasive markers are reassuring but not absolute: if interpretation is uncertain (high-risk activity, athlete), the EP study settles the question.

ecg-tachy-028.question: A 65-year-old man with a history of extensive anterior myocardial infarction has had palpitations for one hour. Faced with this tracing, which diagnosis should you assume first?
options: Sinus tachycardia with bundle branch block
AVNRT with functional bundle branch block
commentaires: Incorrect: possible in theory, but a small minority in ischaemic heart disease; it should never be the first assumption.
Incorrect: no sinus P wave precedes the QRS complexes, and the ischaemic context points to VT.
Correct: regular wide-QRS tachycardia after myocardial infarction: VT until proven otherwise.
Incorrect: a dangerous overdiagnosis in structural heart disease; VT must be considered first.
ecg-tachy-028.explication: On this tracing the tachycardia is regular with wide QRS complexes at around 180 bpm. Faced with a regular wide-QRS tachycardia, the rule is to regard it as VT until proven otherwise, especially in ischaemic heart disease, where over 80 to 90% of wide-QRS tachycardias are VT. SVT with aberrancy does occur, but overdiagnosing it exposes the patient to dangerous treatments (notably IV calcium channel blockers). A history of myocardial infarction is on its own a strong argument for VT. ECG criteria (AV dissociation, morphology, algorithms) then refine the diagnosis.
ecg-tachy-028.aRetenir: Wide-QRS tachycardia in structural heart disease = VT until proven otherwise.
ecg-tachy-028.rappel: A wide-QRS tachycardia (≥ 120 ms) has four mechanisms: VT, SVT with pre-existing or functional bundle branch block (aberrancy), pre-excited SVT (antidromic AVRT, AF or flutter conducted over an accessory pathway) and paced rhythm. Toxic or metabolic causes (hyperkalaemia, sodium channel blockers) also widen the QRS. Good haemodynamic tolerance does not exclude VT. Intravenous calcium channel blockers are dangerous in VT (circulatory collapse) and should be avoided in any wide-QRS tachycardia of uncertain diagnosis. Comparison with a previous ECG in sinus rhythm is very helpful.

ecg-tachy-029.question: A haemodynamically well-tolerated wide-QRS tachycardia is probably supraventricular in origin.
commentaires: Incorrect: haemodynamic tolerance is of no value in distinguishing VT from SVT; many VTs are well tolerated.
Correct: many VTs are tolerated for hours; the diagnosis relies on the clinical context and the ECG.
ecg-tachy-029.explication: Haemodynamic tolerance is of no value in distinguishing VT from SVT with aberrancy. Many VTs, particularly slow ones or those in a relatively preserved heart, are perfectly well tolerated for hours. Conversely, a very fast SVT in a patient with impaired LV function may be poorly tolerated. This is a classic trap that leads to the inappropriate injection of a calcium channel blocker, which can cause circulatory collapse. The diagnosis relies on the context (structural heart disease) and analysis of the 12-lead ECG.
ecg-tachy-029.aRetenir: Good tolerance does not mean SVT.
ecg-tachy-029.rappel: The tolerance of a tachycardia depends mainly on its rate, LV function, loss of atrial contribution and vascular status, not on its mechanism. Slow VT with fairly preserved LV function may be asymptomatic; a fast SVT with impaired LV function may cause cardiogenic shock. In a well-tolerated wide-QRS tachycardia, a 12-lead ECG is recorded before any treatment. The 2022 ESC guidelines favour electrical cardioversion under sedation, if the anaesthetic risk is low, for well-tolerated VT with structural heart disease; intravenous antiarrhythmic drugs (procainamide, amiodarone) are alternatives.

ecg-tachy-030.question: Which of these findings on a regular wide-QRS tachycardia is the most specific for VT?
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the very definition of a wide-QRS tachycardia; it discriminates nothing.
Correct: virtually pathognomonic of VT, but visible in only 20 to 50% of cases.
Incorrect: rate does not distinguish VT from SVT.
Incorrect: a normal axis is not an argument for VT.
ecg-tachy-030.explication: AV dissociation (independent P waves, slower than the QRS complexes) is virtually pathognomonic of VT: it shows that the tachycardia arises below the AV node without activating the atria. However, it is visible in only about 20 to 50% of VTs, so its absence rules nothing out (1:1 retrograde conduction is often present). QRS width alone is not discriminating (a QRS > 160 ms with an LBBB-like pattern or > 140 ms with an RBBB-like pattern is an argument, but a weak one). Rate does not distinguish VT from SVT. A normal axis is not an argument for VT.
ecg-tachy-030.aRetenir: AV dissociation = VT, but its absence does not rule out VT.
ecg-tachy-030.rappel: AV dissociation should be sought in lead II, V1 and the leads where the P wave is largest: regular P waves, slower than the QRS complexes, "marching through" the tachycardia with no fixed relationship to them. At the bedside it also causes jugular cannon "a" waves, a variable first heart sound and beat-to-beat variation in blood pressure. In VT, 1:1 retrograde VA conduction, or VA Wenckebach, is possible and does not exclude VT. An oesophageal or intracardiac lead can reveal atrial activity that is invisible on the surface ECG.

ecg-tachy-031.question: During a regular wide-QRS tachycardia, a single narrow premature complex appears, identical in morphology to the previous sinus QRS complexes. What is it called and what does it mean?
options: A conducted premature atrial beat, favouring SVT
A fusion beat, favouring SVT with aberrancy
Ashman phenomenon, of no diagnostic value
A capture beat, proving AV dissociation and so VT
commentaires: Incorrect: no premature P wave is described, and a narrow complex within a wide tachycardia indicates dissociation.
Incorrect: a fusion beat has an intermediate morphology, and it too points to VT.
Incorrect: Ashman phenomenon produces a wide complex in a narrow-QRS rhythm, not the reverse.
Correct: an independent sinus P wave traverses the AV node and activates the ventricles normally: a narrow, premature complex.
ecg-tachy-031.explication: A capture beat occurs when a sinus P wave, independent of the tachycardia, manages to traverse the AV node and activate the ventricles via the normal His–Purkinje system: the complex is narrow and premature. A fusion beat, of intermediate morphology, results from simultaneous ventricular activation by the VT and by a sinus impulse. Capture and fusion beats are indirect evidence of AV dissociation and therefore of VT (Wellens criteria). They are more common in slow VTs, which give the sinus impulse time to get through. A conducted PAC would be preceded by a premature P wave, and Ashman phenomenon, conversely, produces a wide complex within a narrow-QRS rhythm.
ecg-tachy-031.aRetenir: Capture and fusion beats = AV dissociation = VT.
ecg-tachy-031.rappel: The Wellens criteria (1978) laid the foundations of the differential diagnosis of wide-QRS tachycardia: QRS width (> 140 ms with RBBB morphology, > 160 ms with LBBB morphology), left axis deviation, AV dissociation with its markers (capture and fusion beats) and QRS morphology in V1 and V6. A capture or fusion beat occurs only if a sinus impulse reaches the ventricles outside their refractory period, which explains why they are rare at fast rates. An isolated narrow complex within a wide-QRS tachycardia should always prompt a search for AV dissociation.

ecg-tachy-032.question: List, in order, the four steps of the Brugada algorithm (1991) for diagnosing regular wide-QRS tachycardias.
ecg-tachy-032.reponseAttendue: 1) Absence of an RS complex in all precordial leads → VT. 2) R-to-S interval (onset of R to nadir of S) > 100 ms in at least one precordial lead → VT. 3) AV dissociation → VT. 4) Morphological criteria for VT present in both V1–V2 and V6 → VT. If no step is positive: SVT with aberrancy.
ecg-tachy-032.explication: The Brugada algorithm is sequential: as soon as one step is positive, VT is diagnosed. Complete absence of RS in the precordial leads (QS, monophasic R or qR throughout) and an RS interval > 100 ms reflect slow initial cell-to-cell ventricular activation, characteristic of VT. AV dissociation is the most specific criterion. The morphological criteria of the last step are those of Wellens and Kindwall. Its originally reported sensitivity (~99%) was lower in subsequent validation studies, and it performs less well in antidromic AVRT or on antiarrhythmic drugs.
ecg-tachy-032.aRetenir: Brugada 1991: absence of RS, RS > 100 ms, AV dissociation, morphology in V1–V2 and V6.
ecg-tachy-032.rappel: All diagnostic algorithms for wide-QRS tachycardia share one principle: in aberrant SVT, ventricular activation starts via the His–Purkinje system and is initially fast; in VT, it arises in the myocardium and spreads slowly from cell to cell. In everyday practice their accuracy is lower than in the original studies, and they are misled by pre-excited tachycardias, sodium channel blockers and heart disease with diffuse slow conduction. The clinical context (heart disease, previous infarction) and comparison with the baseline ECG remain decisive; when in doubt, the tachycardia is treated as VT.

ecg-tachy-033.question: In the Brugada algorithm, how is the R-to-S interval measured and which threshold points to VT?
options: From onset of R to peak of R; > 50 ms
From onset of R to nadir of S; > 100 ms
From nadir of S to end of QRS; > 80 ms
From onset of P to onset of QRS; > 200 ms
commentaires: Incorrect: a time to R-wave peak ≥ 50 ms in lead II is the Pava criterion, not the Brugada RS interval.
Correct: an RS > 100 ms in at least one precordial lead reflects slow initial cell-to-cell activation.
Incorrect: this is not the Brugada measurement; the terminal QRS is also slow in bundle branch block.
Incorrect: that is a PR interval, unrelated to the Brugada algorithm.
ecg-tachy-033.explication: The RS interval is measured from the onset of the R wave to the deepest point of the S wave, in a precordial lead with an RS complex. An interval > 100 ms in at least one precordial lead points to VT, as it reflects slow initial activation that does not use the Purkinje network. In SVT with bundle branch block, initial activation occurs via the intact bundle branch and is rapid. The time from R onset to R peak in lead II is a different criterion (Pava, ≥ 50 ms). The criterion can only be applied if an RS complex is present in at least one precordial lead.
ecg-tachy-033.aRetenir: RS (R onset → S nadir) > 100 ms in a precordial lead = VT.
ecg-tachy-033.rappel: Several criteria measure the speed of initial QRS activation: RS interval > 100 ms in a precordial lead (Brugada), time to the peak of the first deflection ≥ 50 ms in lead II (Pava), initial r or q wave > 40 ms and vi/vt ratio ≤ 1 in aVR (Vereckei). They give false-positive results when initial activation is slow for another reason: pre-excited tachycardia (delta wave), class IC or IA antiarrhythmic drugs, hyperkalaemia, or extensive scar with pre-existing bundle branch block. Measurement requires precise identification of QRS onset, ideally on several simultaneously recorded leads.

ecg-tachy-034.question: Which of these criteria is NOT part of the Vereckei algorithm based on lead aVR alone (2008)?
options: Initial r or q wave lasting > 40 ms in aVR
Notch on the downstroke of a negative QRS in aVR
commentaires: Incorrect: this is indeed step 2 of the aVR algorithm.
Incorrect: this is step 1 of the aVR algorithm.
Correct: AV dissociation was part of the first Vereckei algorithm (2007), not the aVR algorithm.
Incorrect: this is step 3 of the aVR algorithm.
ecg-tachy-034.explication: The Vereckei aVR algorithm has four steps, all in aVR: 1) initial R wave → VT; 2) initial r or q wave > 40 ms → VT; 3) notch on the descending limb of a negative-onset, predominantly negative QRS → VT; 4) vi/vt ratio ≤ 1 → VT. The principle is that in SVT with aberrancy, initial (septal) activation moves rapidly away from aVR, producing a fast, negative initial deflection. AV dissociation was the first step of the first Vereckei algorithm (2007, which used the whole ECG), but does not feature in the aVR algorithm.
ecg-tachy-034.aRetenir: aVR algorithm: initial R, initial r/q > 40 ms, notched downstroke, vi/vt ≤ 1.
ecg-tachy-034.rappel: Lead aVR "looks" at the heart from the right shoulder, towards the RV base and outflow tract. With supraventricular conduction, normal or aberrant, initial septal and ventricular activation moves rapidly away from it: the QRS starts with a brief negative deflection. An initial R wave in aVR reflects activation arising at the apex or inferior wall and travelling upwards and to the right, which does not occur with bundle branch block. The first Vereckei algorithm (2007) used the whole ECG: AV dissociation, initial R wave in aVR, morphology matching neither a bundle branch nor a fascicular block, then vi/vt ≤ 1.

ecg-tachy-035.question: In the Vereckei algorithms, what does a vi/vt ratio ≤ 1 indicate?
options: Slower initial than terminal activation: VT
Faster initial activation: SVT with bundle branch block
P-wave voltage lower than T-wave voltage: VT
A short QT interval, favouring SVT with aberrancy
commentaires: Correct: vi is low because activation starts slowly in the myocardium: vi/vt ≤ 1 = VT.
Incorrect: fast initial activation gives vi/vt > 1; this is the opposite of the criterion.
Incorrect: v refers to the QRS voltage excursion (first and last 40 ms), not to the P and T waves.
Incorrect: the vi/vt ratio has nothing to do with the QT interval.
ecg-tachy-035.explication: vi is the voltage excursion (in mV) during the first 40 ms of the QRS, and vt that during the last 40 ms. In SVT with aberrancy, initial activation uses the fast His–Purkinje system (high vi) and it is the terminal portion, related to the block, that is slow: vi/vt > 1. In VT, activation starts in the myocardium, cell to cell, and therefore slowly (low vi), then accelerates as it may reach the Purkinje network: vi/vt ≤ 1. This criterion can fail when there is scar at the terminal exit site, or in fascicular VTs or VTs exiting close to the Purkinje network.
ecg-tachy-035.rappel: The vi/vt ratio is measured on a complex whose QRS onset and end are clearly identifiable: the absolute vertical excursion of the tracing (in mV) is measured during the first 40 ms (vi) and the last 40 ms (vt). It compares conduction velocity at the beginning and end of ventricular activation, regardless of morphology. It may wrongly favour VT when aberrant SVT occurs with septal scar (slowed initial activation), and wrongly favour SVT when VT rapidly engages the Purkinje network. Like the other criteria, it is interpreted in the light of the clinical context.

ecg-tachy-036.question: According to the Pava criterion (2010), which interval from QRS onset to the peak of the first wave (positive or negative) in lead II points to VT?
commentaires: Incorrect: this threshold is too low and lacks specificity.
Correct: an interval ≥ 50 ms to the peak of the first deflection in lead II points to VT (Pava 2010).
Incorrect: this is not the Pava threshold.
Incorrect: 100 ms is the threshold for the Brugada RS interval in the precordial leads.
ecg-tachy-036.explication: The Pava criterion measures the R-wave peak time in lead II: the interval between QRS onset and the first change in polarity (peak of the first deflection, whether positive or negative). An interval ≥ 50 ms favours VT. Like the Brugada RS criterion or the Vereckei vi/vt ratio, it exploits the fact that VT begins with slow myocardial activation. Its appeal is its simplicity (one lead, a single number), but it remains one argument among others, with variable sensitivity across validation studies. The 100 ms threshold corresponds to the Brugada RS interval in the precordial leads.
ecg-tachy-036.aRetenir: Peak of the first wave in lead II ≥ 50 ms = VT (Pava criterion).
ecg-tachy-036.rappel: The R-wave peak time in lead II is measured from QRS onset to the first change in polarity, whether the first deflection is positive or negative. Lead II is chosen because it is recorded on almost every tracing and QRS onset is often clear in it. No single criterion is sensitive enough to exclude VT: criteria of initial activation, morphology and AV dissociation are combined, and the clinical context (age, structural heart disease, previous infarction) carries as much weight as the ECG. The 2022 ESC guidelines state that a wide-QRS tachycardia should be regarded as VT until proven otherwise.

ecg-tachy-037.question: Wide-QRS tachycardia with an RBBB-like pattern (positive QRS in V1). Which morphological criteria favour VT?
options: V1: monophasic R wave or qR complex
commentaires: Correct: a monophasic R, qR or Rr' in V1 reflects abnormal initial activation: VT.
Correct: R/S < 1 or QS in V6: activation moves away from the left lateral wall.
Incorrect: a triphasic rsR' is the typical pattern of SVT with right bundle branch block.
Incorrect: a qRs with R/S > 1 in V6 is typical of RBBB-type aberrant conduction.
ecg-tachy-037.explication: With an RBBB-like pattern, SVT with right bundle branch block retains normal initial activation: triphasic rsR' in V1 and qRs with R/S > 1 in V6. In VT, V1 shows a monophasic R wave, a qR complex or an Rr' pattern (taller "left rabbit ear"), and V6 shows an R/S ratio < 1 or a QS pattern, reflecting activation moving away from the left lateral wall. These Wellens criteria, incorporated by Brugada, complement the interval criteria. A typical bundle branch block pattern is not, however, enough to rule out fascicular or bundle branch re-entrant VT.
ecg-tachy-037.aRetenir: RBBB-like pattern: monophasic R/qR in V1 and R/S < 1 in V6 = VT.
ecg-tachy-037.rappel: The morphology of VT reflects its exit site. RBBB morphology (positive QRS in V1) indicates a left ventricular exit, as the LV is activated before the RV. LBBB morphology (negative QRS in V1) indicates an RV or left septal exit. The frontal axis refines the height: inferior axis for a basal or outflow tract exit, superior axis for an inferior or apical exit. Idiopathic fascicular VT (left posterior fascicle exit) classically produces RBBB morphology with left axis deviation and relatively narrow QRS complexes, and is sensitive to verapamil.

ecg-tachy-038.question: Wide-QRS tachycardia with an LBBB-like pattern (negative QRS in V1). Which of these (Kindwall) criteria favours VT?
options: Narrow S wave with a rapid downstroke in V1
Monophasic R wave in V6 with no q wave
QRS onset to S-wave nadir < 60 ms in V1
R-wave duration > 30 ms in V1 or V2
commentaires: Incorrect: an S wave with a rapid, smooth downstroke is the pattern of typical LBBB, favouring SVT with aberrancy.
Incorrect: a monophasic R without q in V6 is the LBBB pattern; it is a Q wave in V6 that points to VT.
Incorrect: it is an interval > 60 ms that points to VT.
Correct: Kindwall criterion; a broad initial R wave in V1–V2 reflects slow initial activation.
ecg-tachy-038.explication: Kindwall and Josephson described four VT criteria in LBBB-like patterns: R wave > 30 ms in V1 or V2, notching of the S-wave downstroke in V1–V2, QRS onset to S-wave nadir > 60 ms in V1 or V2, and a Q wave in V6. In SVT with left bundle branch block, initial septal activation is rapid: narrow r wave, S wave with a rapid, smooth downstroke, and monophasic R without q in V6. A rapid S-wave downstroke, a short interval and a monophasic R without q in V6 therefore describe a "typical" LBBB pattern, favouring SVT with aberrancy.
ecg-tachy-038.aRetenir: LBBB-like pattern: R > 30 ms in V1–V2, notched S, interval > 60 ms or Q in V6 = VT.
ecg-tachy-038.rappel: In true LBBB, the LV is activated from the right bundle branch across the septum: initial activation remains fast, hence a narrow r wave in V1 and a steep S wave, then a broad monophasic R wave in V6. Slow initial activation in V1–V2 or a Q wave in V6 contradicts this pattern and points to VT. VTs with LBBB morphology arise from the RV (outflow tract, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy) or the septum. Bundle branch re-entrant VT, which uses the conduction system, can produce a typical LBBB pattern: it occurs mainly in cardiomyopathy with pre-existing conduction disease.

ecg-tachy-039.question: Positive QRS concordance from V1 to V6 (all predominantly positive) is pathognomonic of VT.
commentaires: Incorrect: highly specific but not absolute; a pre-excited tachycardia via a left posterior pathway also produces positive concordance.
Correct: positive concordance can occur in antidromic AVRT or pre-excited AF via a left posterior pathway.
ecg-tachy-039.explication: Precordial concordance (all QRS complexes of the same polarity from V1 to V6) is a highly specific criterion for VT, but not an absolute one. Negative concordance (QS throughout) is virtually pathognomonic of VT with an anterior/apical exit. Positive concordance, however, can be seen with a pre-excited tachycardia (antidromic AVRT or AF/flutter conducted over a left posterior accessory pathway), since activation starts at the posterior LV base and travels anteriorly. The context (known pre-excitation) and the sinus rhythm ECG are then decisive.
ecg-tachy-039.aRetenir: Positive concordance: usually VT, but consider a pre-excited tachycardia via a left posterior pathway.
ecg-tachy-039.rappel: The polarity of the precordial QRS complexes shows the anteroposterior direction of activation: activation starting at the posterior base and travelling towards the apex and anteriorly produces positive QRS complexes from V1 to V6, whereas activation starting at the anterior apex produces negative ones. Concordance is present only if all six precordial leads are monophasic and of the same polarity (R or QS), with no RS complex. Absence of concordance does not exclude VT. Positive concordance in VT reflects a basal exit, from the posterior or perimitral LV, close to the insertion of left posterior accessory pathways.

ecg-tachy-040.question: Wide-QRS tachycardia with an axis between −90° and ±180° (QRS negative in I and aVF). What is the significance of this sign?
options: It is typical of orthodromic AVRT
It points to SVT with right bundle branch block
commentaires: Incorrect: orthodromic AVRT has narrow QRS complexes, or a typical bundle branch block pattern with aberrancy.
Incorrect: bundle branch or fascicular block deviates the axis to the left or right, not into this quadrant.
Correct: an extreme (northwest) axis is almost never seen with aberrant conduction: activation starts at the apex.
Incorrect: it is a classic morphological criterion for VT, even though its absence rules nothing out.
ecg-tachy-040.explication: An extreme or "indeterminate" axis (right superior quadrant, sometimes called "no man's land" or northwest axis) is almost never seen with aberrant conduction, because bundle branch or fascicular block deviates the axis to the left or right, but not into this zone. It reflects activation starting at the apex and travelling towards the base and to the right, favouring VT. It is a classic morphological criterion, in line with Wellens' work on axis deviation. Its absence does not rule out VT. Severe hyperkalaemia or class IC drugs can, however, produce bizarre axes.
ecg-tachy-040.aRetenir: Axis between −90° and ±180° during a wide-QRS tachycardia = VT.
ecg-tachy-040.rappel: The frontal axis is quickly located from QRS polarity in leads I and aVF: I and aVF positive, normal axis (0 to +90°); I positive and aVF negative, left axis; I negative and aVF positive, right axis; I and aVF negative, right superior quadrant (-90° to ±180°). Bundle branch and fascicular blocks shift the axis but do not bring it into this quadrant. During a wide-QRS tachycardia, left axis deviation combined with RBBB morphology also favours VT. Comparing the axis with that of the ECG in sinus rhythm provides an additional clue.

ecg-tachy-041.question: Name three mechanisms by which a tachycardia of supraventricular origin can present with wide QRS complexes.
ecg-tachy-041.reponseAttendue: 1) Pre-existing or functional bundle branch block (rate-dependent aberrant conduction). 2) Anterograde conduction over an accessory pathway (antidromic AVRT, pre-excited AF/flutter/atrial tachycardia). 3) Non-specific QRS widening: class IC/IA antiarrhythmic drugs (use-dependent effect), hyperkalaemia. (Also acceptable: ventricular pacing tracking an atrial tachycardia in a pacemaker patient.)
ecg-tachy-041.explication: A supraventricular tachycardia produces wide QRS complexes when ventricular activation does not proceed normally through both bundle branches. This is the case with permanent or functional bundle branch block (aberrancy), anterograde conduction over an accessory pathway (maximal pre-excitation), and diffuse slowing of intraventricular conduction due to sodium channel blockers or hyperkalaemia. In a patient with a dual-chamber pacemaker, an atrial tachycardia tracked by the device up to the upper rate also produces wide paced QRS complexes. These situations account for only a minority of wide-QRS tachycardias, particularly in structural heart disease.
ecg-tachy-041.aRetenir: Wide-QRS SVT: aberrancy, pre-excitation, or drug-induced/metabolic widening.
ecg-tachy-041.rappel: Rate-dependent aberrancy occurs when the cycle length shortens below the refractory period of a bundle branch (phase 3); it more often affects the right bundle branch and may disappear when the tachycardia slows. If the bundle branch block is pre-existing, QRS morphology during tachycardia is identical to that in sinus rhythm: comparison with the baseline ECG is the strongest argument. Antidromic AVRT conducts down the accessory pathway and back up the AV node: the QRS is fully pre-excited. In a patient with a dual-chamber pacemaker, an atrial tachycardia tracked by the device produces paced QRS complexes at the maximum tracking rate.

ecg-tachy-042.question: A 70-year-old patient is confused and pale, BP 70/40 mmHg. The monitor shows this tracing. What is the immediate management?
options: IV amiodarone over 30 minutes, then reassessment
Vagal manoeuvres, then an IV adenosine bolus
Slow IV verapamil with blood pressure monitoring
commentaires: Incorrect: IV antiarrhythmic drugs are reserved for well-tolerated tachycardias; they delay the life-saving intervention.
