Correct: poorly tolerated tachycardia (hypotension, confusion): immediate synchronised cardioversion, whatever the mechanism.
Incorrect: no first-line role in a poorly tolerated wide-QRS tachycardia.
Incorrect: contraindicated in an undiagnosed wide-QRS tachycardia: risk of circulatory collapse.
ecg-tachy-042.explication: On this tracing the tachycardia is regular with wide QRS complexes at around 200 bpm. Any poorly tolerated wide-QRS tachycardia (hypotension, impaired consciousness, chest pain, acute heart failure) calls for immediate electrical cardioversion, synchronised to the QRS, under brief sedation, whatever the mechanism. IV antiarrhythmic drugs are reserved for tolerated tachycardias. Vagal manoeuvres and adenosine have no first-line role here. IV verapamil is contraindicated in an undiagnosed wide-QRS tachycardia, with a risk of circulatory collapse. If there is no pulse, the cardiac arrest algorithm applies (unsynchronised shock).
ecg-tachy-042.aRetenir: Poorly tolerated tachycardia = immediate synchronised electrical cardioversion.
ecg-tachy-042.rappel: Synchronised cardioversion delivers the shock on the sensed R wave, to avoid the vulnerable period of the T wave, when a shock can trigger VF. It is performed under brief sedation, with adhesive pads in the anterolateral or anteroposterior position, checking that the synchronisation marker falls on each QRS and not on the T wave. Many defibrillators revert to unsynchronised mode after each shock: synchronisation must be re-enabled before another shock. In pulseless VT or VF, or if synchronisation is impossible (polymorphic QRS complexes), an unsynchronised shock is delivered.

ecg-tachy-043.question: A 60-year-old man has well-tolerated palpitations; tracing below, mechanism uncertain. Which treatment must be avoided?
options: IV verapamil as a slow bolus
commentaires: Correct: in an undiagnosed wide-QRS tachycardia, it can cause abrupt hypotension and VF.
Incorrect: proposed by the 2022 ESC guidelines in stable patients (not widely available in France).
Incorrect: a possible option, particularly in structural heart disease.
Incorrect: elective electrical cardioversion is a safe option in a stable patient.
ecg-tachy-043.explication: IV rate-limiting calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) are contraindicated in an undiagnosed wide-QRS tachycardia: if it is VT, they can cause abrupt hypotension and deterioration into VF. In stable patients, the 2022 ESC guidelines propose electrical cardioversion or an IV antiarrhythmic drug such as procainamide (not widely available in France), or amiodarone (particularly in structural heart disease). The main exception is idiopathic fascicular VT, which is verapamil-sensitive, but its diagnosis requires expert analysis of the tracing. Adenosine may be considered only in the absence of pre-excitation and when SVT with aberrancy is strongly suspected.
ecg-tachy-043.aRetenir: No verapamil for an undiagnosed wide-QRS tachycardia.
ecg-tachy-043.rappel: In VT with structural heart disease, cardiac output depends on already impaired contractility and compensatory vascular tone: verapamil and diltiazem, which are negatively inotropic and vasodilating, may cause circulatory collapse, itself a source of ischaemia and degeneration into VF. Each intravenous antiarrhythmic drug used in tolerated VT has its limits: procainamide (a sodium channel blocker) widens the QRS and may cause hypotension; amiodarone acts more slowly to terminate VT but helps prevent recurrences. Whatever the choice, preparation for electrical cardioversion should accompany any pharmacological treatment.

ecg-tachy-044.question: How is a wide-QRS tachycardia defined?
ecg-tachy-044.reponseAttendue: A tachycardia with a rate > 100 bpm and a QRS duration ≥ 120 ms.
ecg-tachy-044.explication: A tachycardia is described as wide-QRS when the rate exceeds 100 bpm and the QRS duration is at least 120 ms. This definition is purely descriptive: it includes VT, but also SVT conducted with bundle branch block, pre-excited tachycardias and tachycardias widened by drugs or hyperkalaemia. In practice, the safety rule is to treat it as VT until the diagnosis is established. A 12-lead ECG should always be recorded if the patient's condition allows, as it is essential for diagnosis and for any subsequent ablation.
ecg-tachy-044.aRetenir: Wide-QRS tachycardia = HR > 100 bpm and QRS ≥ 120 ms.
ecg-tachy-044.rappel: QRS duration is measured on the 12 simultaneously recorded leads, from the earliest onset to the latest offset, because part of the QRS may be isoelectric in a single lead and lead to underestimating its width. In adults, a normal QRS lasts less than 110–120 ms; between 110 and 119 ms, the term incomplete intraventricular conduction delay is used. Tachycardia is defined as a rate > 100 bpm. Measuring on a single monitor or Holter lead is a source of error: a QRS that looks narrow in one lead may be wide on the 12-lead ECG.

ecg-tachy-045.question: In a regular wide-QRS tachycardia, which findings favour VT?
options: Triphasic rsR' in V1, typical of right bundle branch block
commentaires: Correct: the most specific criterion for VT.
Correct: indirect markers of AV dissociation, and therefore of VT.
Incorrect: this pattern reflects normal initial activation and rather points to SVT with aberrancy.
Incorrect: tolerance has no diagnostic value; many VTs are well tolerated.
ecg-tachy-045.explication: AV dissociation, and its indirect markers, capture and fusion beats, are the most specific criteria for VT. QRS concordance from V1 to V6, especially negative, is also highly specific. Conversely, a triphasic rsR' pattern in V1, typical of right bundle branch block, reflects normal initial activation and rather points to SVT with aberrancy. Haemodynamic tolerance has no diagnostic value: many VTs are well tolerated. The context (ischaemic heart disease, prior myocardial infarction) is often the most powerful argument.
ecg-tachy-045.aRetenir: AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, concordance: VT; tolerance proves nothing.
ecg-tachy-045.rappel: ECG clues in a wide-QRS tachycardia do not all carry the same weight. Highly specific for VT: AV dissociation, capture and fusion beats, negative precordial concordance, and an axis in the right superior quadrant. Of intermediate value: morphological criteria in V1–V2 and V6, and slow initial activation. Poorly discriminating: QRS width alone, rate and regularity. The ratio of atrial to ventricular activity is also informative: more QRS complexes than P waves points to VT, more P waves than QRS complexes to atrial tachycardia or flutter. No SVT sign is sensitive enough to rule out VT.

ecg-tachy-046.question: A 35-year-old woman with a structurally normal heart on echocardiography has runs of exercise-induced monomorphic VT: LBBB-like pattern, inferior axis (positive QRS in II, III, aVF), precordial transition in V4. What is the most likely origin?
commentaires: Incorrect: posterior fascicular VT produces an RBBB-like pattern with left axis deviation.
Incorrect: scar-related VT implies structural heart disease, absent here; its axis would be superior.
Incorrect: a mitral origin produces an RBBB-like pattern (positive in V1).
Correct: LBBB-like pattern + inferior axis + late transition (≥ V4) in a normal heart: RVOT VT.
ecg-tachy-046.explication: The combination of an LBBB-like pattern (negative in V1) and an inferior axis reflects a superior origin, in the outflow tracts. A late transition (V4 or beyond) points to the RV outflow tract, the most common form of idiopathic VT. These VTs typically occur on exertion or under stress (cAMP-mediated triggered activity). Posterior fascicular VT produces an RBBB-like pattern with left axis deviation. Scar-related VT implies structural heart disease. Before accepting an idiopathic form, ARVC must be excluded (MRI, baseline ECG, signal-averaged ECG).
ecg-tachy-046.aRetenir: LBBB-like pattern + inferior axis + transition ≥ V4 in a normal heart: RVOT VT.
ecg-tachy-046.rappel: Idiopathic outflow tract VT and PVCs occur in structurally normal hearts and usually carry a good prognosis. They present as frequent PVCs, repetitive monomorphic salvos or sustained VT, often favoured by exercise, stress or the recovery phase. A high PVC burden can nevertheless induce a cardiomyopathy, which is reversible after suppression. Treatment combines a beta-blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with catheter ablation, which is a first-line option for symptomatic right ventricular outflow tract forms, with a high success rate.

ecg-tachy-047.question: Outflow tract PVCs with a precordial transition in V3, whereas the transition in sinus rhythm is in V4. The V2 transition ratio (Betensky) is 0.7. What is the most likely origin?
options: Right outflow tract, anterior free wall
commentaires: Correct: PVC with V3 transition and a V2 transition ratio ≥ 0.60: left-sided origin (≈ 90% accuracy).
Incorrect: a free-wall origin produces a late transition and wider, notched QRS complexes.
Incorrect: a V2 transition ratio of 0.7, with a transition earlier than in sinus rhythm, points to the left.
Incorrect: fascicular VT produces an RBBB-like pattern, not an outflow tract pattern.
ecg-tachy-047.explication: When the PVC transition is in V3, distinguishing between right and left outflow tracts is difficult. Betensky proposed comparing the R-wave percentage in V2 [R/(R+S)] during the PVC with that in sinus rhythm. In patients whose PVC transitions in V3, a ratio ≥ 0.60 predicts a left-sided origin with good accuracy (about 90%). Conversely, a PVC transition later than the sinus transition virtually excludes a left-sided origin; here the PVC transition (V3) is earlier than the sinus rhythm transition (V4), which is consistent with the ratio of 0.7. This helps the operator prepare for a retrograde aortic or transseptal approach.
ecg-tachy-047.aRetenir: V2 transition ratio ≥ 0.60 = left outflow tract origin.
ecg-tachy-047.rappel: The outflow tracts are intertwined: the RVOT lies anterior and to the left of the LVOT, whose aortic cusps (right and left coronary) are posterior. The more posterior the origin, the earlier the precordial transition; this is why a transition at or before V2 points to the left side, at or after V4 to the right, with V3 remaining a grey zone. In lead I, a negative deflection indicates a more leftward origin (anterior septum below the pulmonary valve, left coronary cusp). Comparison with the transition in sinus rhythm corrects for the position of the heart in the chest.

ecg-tachy-048.question: A 22-year-old man with a structurally normal heart. Regular VT at 170 bpm, QRS 130 ms, RBBB-like pattern with left axis deviation ("RBBB + left anterior fascicular block" pattern). It terminates with IV verapamil. What is the diagnosis?
commentaires: Incorrect: RVOT VT produces an LBBB-like pattern with an inferior axis.
Incorrect: a classic trap; verapamil sensitivity and the patient profile do not allow SVT to be concluded.
Correct: RBBB-like pattern, left axis, only mildly widened QRS, young patient with a normal heart and verapamil sensitivity: Belhassen VT.
Incorrect: bundle branch re-entrant VT occurs in structural heart disease with conduction disease, not in a normal heart.
ecg-tachy-048.explication: Idiopathic left fascicular VT (described by Belhassen) is a re-entry involving the Purkinje network of the left posterior fascicle. The pattern is RBBB-like with left axis deviation, and the QRS is relatively narrow (often 120–140 ms) because activation rapidly engages the Purkinje network. It occurs in young people with structurally normal hearts and is verapamil-sensitive, which distinguishes it from most VTs. Its morphology often leads to it being mistaken for SVT with aberrancy. Bundle branch re-entrant VT, by contrast, occurs in structural heart disease with conduction disease. The rarer anterior fascicular form produces an RBBB-like pattern with right axis deviation.
ecg-tachy-048.aRetenir: RBBB-like pattern + left axis + mildly wide QRS + young patient + verapamil-sensitive = left posterior fascicular VT.
ecg-tachy-048.rappel: Left fascicular VT is a re-entry involving Purkinje tissue with slow, decremental, calcium channel-dependent conduction, hence its sensitivity to verapamil. At EP study, a diastolic potential (P1) and a presystolic Purkinje potential (P2) are recorded along the inferior septum and guide ablation. It is usually inducible by atrial or ventricular programmed stimulation and can be entrained. Acutely, intravenous verapamil terminates it; in the long term, catheter ablation is the curative treatment of recurrent forms, oral verapamil often being insufficient.

ecg-tachy-049.question: Idiopathic outflow tract VT can be terminated by adenosine.
commentaires: Correct: cAMP-mediated triggered activity; adenosine can terminate it, as can beta-blockers.
Incorrect: the statement is true; termination with adenosine therefore does not prove that a wide-QRS tachycardia is SVT.
ecg-tachy-049.explication: Idiopathic outflow tract VTs are most often due to triggered activity from delayed afterdepolarisations, mediated by cAMP and intracellular calcium. Adenosine, by lowering cAMP, can terminate these VTs, as can vagal manoeuvres or beta-blockers. This is a diagnostic trap: termination of a wide-QRS tachycardia with adenosine does not prove that it is SVT. Scar-related re-entrant VTs, by contrast, are not adenosine-sensitive.
ecg-tachy-049.aRetenir: Termination with adenosine does not rule out VT (outflow tract VTs are adenosine-sensitive).
ecg-tachy-049.rappel: Three mechanisms account for VT: re-entry (around scar or within the conduction system), abnormal automaticity, and triggered activity due to early or delayed afterdepolarisations. Re-entry is inducible by programmed extrastimuli, can be entrained and is not sensitive to adenosine. Triggered activity due to delayed afterdepolarisations depends on calcium overload: it is favoured by catecholamines (isoprenaline, exercise), is induced mainly by rapid burst pacing and responds to adenosine, beta-blockers and verapamil. Abnormal automaticity is neither inducible nor terminated by pacing, and responds poorly to adenosine.

ecg-tachy-050.question: A 30-year-old athlete presents with monomorphic VT with an LBBB-like pattern and a superior axis. Which diagnosis must be actively sought?
options: AVNRT with left bundle branch block
commentaires: Incorrect: outflow tract VT has an inferior axis, not a superior one.
Correct: LBBB-like pattern with superior axis = inferior RV exit, a major criterion in the 2010 Task Force criteria.
Incorrect: posterior fascicular VT produces an RBBB-like pattern.
Incorrect: in an athlete with LBBB-like VT, settling for SVT with aberrancy would be dangerous.
ecg-tachy-050.explication: VT with an LBBB-like pattern arises from the RV or the septum. An inferior axis suggests the outflow tract, whereas a superior axis indicates an exit from the inferior wall or the subtricuspid region of the RV, which is not the profile of idiopathic VT. In an athlete, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy must be sought (resting ECG, epsilon wave, T-wave inversion, cardiac MRI, Holter). The diagnosis relies on the 2010 Task Force criteria, in which LBBB-type VT with a superior axis is a major criterion. Cessation of intensive sport is part of management.
ecg-tachy-050.aRetenir: LBBB-like VT with a superior axis: think ARVC; this is not outflow tract VT.
ecg-tachy-050.rappel: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is a genetic disease, most often due to desmosomal genes (plakophilin-2 in particular), with fibro-fatty replacement of the RV myocardium and sometimes the LV. The 2010 Task Force criteria combine structural abnormalities (echocardiography, MRI), histology, repolarisation abnormalities (T-wave inversion in V1 to V3 in individuals over 14 years without complete RBBB, a major criterion), depolarisation abnormalities (epsilon wave, a major criterion), arrhythmias, and family history or genetics. Intense exercise accelerates disease expression and increases arrhythmic risk.

ecg-tachy-051.question: On Holter, the run below lasts 25 seconds in total, terminates spontaneously and is asymptomatic. How is it classified?
commentaires: Incorrect: sustained VT lasts more than 30 s or requires intervention.
Incorrect: AIVR is slower (≈ 50–110 bpm); here the rate is around 140 bpm.
Incorrect: the QRS complexes keep the same morphology from beat to beat.
Correct: wide QRS complexes of stable morphology, duration < 30 s and spontaneous termination without haemodynamic compromise.
ecg-tachy-051.explication: On this tracing the complexes are wide, regular (≈ 140 bpm) and of identical morphology: monomorphic VT. VT is termed sustained if it lasts more than 30 seconds or requires intervention to terminate it (because it is poorly tolerated). Below 30 seconds, from 3 consecutive complexes at more than 100 bpm, it is termed non-sustained VT. It is monomorphic when the QRS morphology is stable, and polymorphic when it changes from beat to beat. Accelerated idioventricular rhythm has a rate of around 50–110 bpm (typically after reperfusion). These 2022 ESC definitions determine prognostic assessment and management.
ecg-tachy-051.aRetenir: Sustained VT = > 30 s or poorly tolerated; otherwise non-sustained.
ecg-tachy-051.rappel: The significance of non-sustained VT depends on the substrate. In a structurally normal heart, monomorphic non-sustained VT, particularly from the outflow tract, is usually benign; with structural heart disease, it is a risk marker that requires investigation (echocardiography, MRI, assessment for ischaemia). Polymorphic non-sustained VT should prompt a search for ischaemia or a channelopathy. The 2022 ESC guidelines also define electrical storm as at least three episodes of sustained VT within 24 hours, and incessant VT as VT that recurs immediately after each termination. Describing VT means stating its duration, morphology, rate and tolerance.

ecg-tachy-052.question: A patient with non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy has left bundle branch block and a long PR interval in sinus rhythm. He develops a fast VT whose LBBB-like morphology closely resembles the sinus QRS. Which mechanism should you suspect and what is its curative treatment?
ecg-tachy-052.reponseAttendue: Bundle branch re-entrant VT (circuit travelling down the right bundle branch and up the left bundle branch); curative treatment: radiofrequency ablation of the right bundle branch (an ICD usually remains indicated because of the underlying cardiomyopathy).
ecg-tachy-052.explication: Bundle branch re-entrant VT uses the His–Purkinje system as its re-entrant circuit, which requires slowed conduction within this system: it typically occurs in dilated cardiomyopathy, after valve surgery or in myotonic dystrophies. The circuit most often travels down the right bundle branch and up the left bundle branch, hence an LBBB-like morphology similar to the sinus left bundle branch block. At EP study, each QRS is preceded by a His potential, with an HV interval often equal to or greater than that in sinus rhythm. Right bundle branch ablation is curative and straightforward, but the myocardial substrate usually warrants an ICD. A pacemaker may be needed if left bundle branch conduction is severely impaired.
ecg-tachy-052.aRetenir: LBBB-like VT identical to the sinus LBBB in DCM: think bundle branch re-entry; ablate the right bundle branch.
ecg-tachy-052.rappel: Re-entry using the His–Purkinje system has three forms: the most common conducts down the right bundle branch and back up the left (LBBB morphology); the reverse form produces RBBB morphology; interfascicular re-entry circulates between the left anterior and posterior fascicles (RBBB morphology with a variable axis). The substrate is slowed conduction in the His–Purkinje system, with a prolonged HV interval in sinus rhythm. At EP study, changes in the H–H interval precede and drive changes in the V–V interval. Ablating the right bundle branch in the presence of pre-existing LBBB exposes to complete AV block and the need for pacing.

ecg-tachy-053.question: A 72-year-old inpatient with a serum potassium of 2.9 mmol/l has recurrent episodes of presyncope. What is the diagnosis on this tracing?
commentaires: Incorrect: VF is chaotic, with no identifiable complexes; here the QRS complexes are organised in spindles.
Correct: polymorphic VT in "spindles" twisting around the baseline, in the setting of hypokalaemia.
Incorrect: QRS morphology and amplitude change cyclically: the VT is polymorphic.
Incorrect: pre-excited AF is an irregular wide-QRS rhythm, but without cyclical twisting or a long baseline QT.
ecg-tachy-053.explication: On this tracing, after a baseline beat with a long QT, a polymorphic wide-QRS tachycardia appears whose amplitude waxes and wanes cyclically, the complexes appearing to twist around the baseline. Torsades de pointes are a particular form of polymorphic VT in which the QRS axis rotates progressively around the isoelectric line, producing a "spindle" appearance. They occur on a background of long QT, congenital or acquired (drugs, hypokalaemia, bradycardia). They are often non-sustained and recurrent, causing syncope, but can degenerate into VF. VF is completely chaotic, with no identifiable complexes. Pre-excited AF is an irregular wide-QRS rhythm but without this cyclical twisting or a long baseline QT.
ecg-tachy-053.aRetenir: Polymorphic VT in "spindles" on a long QT = torsades de pointes.
ecg-tachy-053.rappel: The QT interval is measured from QRS onset to the end of the T wave, ideally in lead II or V5, using the tangent method on the downslope of the T wave and excluding a separate U wave. It is corrected for heart rate (QTc, Bazett formula, unreliable at extreme rates). According to the AHA statement by Drew et al., a QTc > 500 ms or an increase > 60 ms from baseline indicates a high risk of torsades de pointes in hospitalised patients. When the QRS is wide, QT prolongation partly reflects QRS widening and must be interpreted with caution.

ecg-tachy-054.question: A 78-year-old inpatient on hydroxyzine and azithromycin, with a serum potassium of 3.1 mmol/l, has recurrent episodes like the one on this tracing. Which measures are indicated?
commentaires: Correct: first-line treatment of torsades, even if serum magnesium is normal.
Correct: hypokalaemia prolongs the QT; aim for a high-normal potassium of 4.5 to 5 mmol/l.
Correct: both drugs prolong the QT; stopping them is essential.
Incorrect: amiodarone prolongs the QT; it is contraindicated in torsades.
Incorrect: sotalol prolongs the QT and would aggravate the torsades.
ecg-tachy-054.explication: This tracing shows torsades de pointes. Treatment is based on IV magnesium sulphate (typically 2 g as a slow bolus, repeatable), even if serum magnesium is normal. At the same time, all QT-prolonging drugs must be stopped, potassium corrected (target 4.5–5 mmol/l) and, if necessary, the heart rate increased (isoprenaline or temporary pacing) to shorten the QT and abolish pauses. Amiodarone and sotalol prolong the QT: this is the classic trap, and they are contraindicated in torsades. If VF develops, defibrillate.
ecg-tachy-054.aRetenir: Torsades: IV magnesium, potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs, increase the heart rate.
ecg-tachy-054.rappel: Torsades de pointes are triggered by early afterdepolarisations in myocardium with prolonged and heterogeneous repolarisation. Intravenous magnesium acts by suppressing these afterdepolarisations (inhibition of the calcium current), without markedly shortening the QT interval. Increasing the heart rate shortens the QT interval and abolishes pauses: temporary pacing, or isoprenaline in the meantime, the latter to be avoided in congenital long QT syndrome and in ischaemia. Continuous monitoring is required, with a defibrillator at hand, and before any resumption the indication for each QT-prolonging drug must be reassessed.

ecg-tachy-055.question: Which of these factors predispose to torsades de pointes in acquired long QT?
commentaires: Correct: hypokalaemia prolongs repolarisation and predisposes to torsades.
Correct: bradycardia prolongs the QT and creates long–short cycle sequences.
Correct: female sex is a recognised risk factor (physiologically longer QT).
Incorrect: hypercalcaemia shortens the QT.
Incorrect: tachycardia shortens the QT; the heart rate is even increased to treat torsades.
ecg-tachy-055.explication: The main risk factors for acquired torsades are female sex, age, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia (AV block, pauses), underlying heart disease, combinations of several QT-prolonging drugs, drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibitors) and renal or hepatic failure. Bradycardia prolongs the QT and promotes long–short cycle sequences; tachycardia, conversely, shortens the QT, which is why the heart rate is increased to treat torsades. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT (short ST segment). These factors should be reassessed before prescribing any drug that can cause torsades.
ecg-tachy-055.aRetenir: Female sex, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and polypharmacy: the setting for torsades.
ecg-tachy-055.rappel: Most QT-prolonging drugs block the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current IKr (hERG channel): class IA and III antiarrhythmic drugs, some macrolides and fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, methadone, antiemetics, and antihistamines such as hydroxyzine. The risk increases with dose, combination of several drugs, inhibitors of their metabolism and reduced "repolarisation reserve" (concealed congenital long QT, hypertrophy, heart failure). Dedicated databases (CredibleMeds) classify drugs by risk. An ECG before and after initiation is recommended in patients at risk.

ecg-tachy-056.question: Which initiating sequence is typical of the onset of torsades de pointes in acquired long QT?
options: Gradual acceleration of the sinus rate
Very early R-on-T premature beat with no preceding pause
commentaires: Incorrect: acceleration of the heart rate shortens the QT and protects against acquired torsades.
Incorrect: this suggests "short-coupled" torsades with a normal QT, a rare and distinct entity.
Correct: premature beat, compensatory pause that prolongs the QT, then another early premature beat: pause-dependent torsades.
Incorrect: adrenergic triggering on exercise is more characteristic of congenital long QT type 1.
ecg-tachy-056.explication: Acquired ("pause-dependent") torsades are typically initiated by a short–long–short sequence: a premature beat (short cycle) followed by a compensatory pause (long cycle), which further prolongs the QT of the next beat, then another early premature beat that triggers the torsades. This is why increasing the heart rate (isoprenaline, pacing) is effective. Adrenergic acceleration on exercise is instead the typical trigger of congenital long QT type 1 ("adrenergic-dependent" forms). A very early (R-on-T) premature beat with no preceding pause, with a normal QT, rather suggests "short-coupled" torsades de pointes, a rare and distinct entity.
ecg-tachy-056.rappel: In acquired long QT, a pause prolongs the action potential of the following beat and increases dispersion of repolarisation; early afterdepolarisations then arise in late phase 2 or phase 3 and trigger functional re-entry. In congenital long QT syndromes, triggers depend on genotype: exercise, particularly swimming, in LQT1; emotion or a sudden auditory stimulus (alarm clock) in LQT2; rest or sleep in LQT3. This distinction guides prevention: increasing the heart rate in pause-dependent forms, beta-blockers in adrenergic forms.

ecg-tachy-057.question: A 58-year-old man with chest pain for one hour has recurrent polymorphic VT with a normal QT between episodes and has been cardioverted. What is the diagnostic priority?
commentaires: Correct: recurrent polymorphic VT with a normal QT and chest pain: acute ischaemia until proven otherwise.
Incorrect: an ajmaline challenge is only considered once an ischaemic or structural cause has been excluded.
Incorrect: the QT is normal; genetics is not a priority in the setting of chest pain.
Incorrect: the episodes are already documented; it is the cause that must be treated urgently.
ecg-tachy-057.explication: Polymorphic VT (or VF) with a normal QT should first raise the suspicion of acute myocardial ischaemia, the main mechanism of polymorphic VT in adults. The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend urgent coronary angiography (and revascularisation) in patients with recurrent polymorphic VT or VF suggestive of ischaemia. Torsades de pointes, by contrast, occur with a long QT. An ajmaline challenge or genetic testing is only considered after excluding a structural or ischaemic cause. Beta-blockers and IV amiodarone are useful for recurrences.
ecg-tachy-057.aRetenir: Polymorphic VT with a normal QT: acute ischaemia until proven otherwise → coronary angiography.
ecg-tachy-057.rappel: Polymorphic VT is distinguished from torsades de pointes by a normal QT interval between episodes. In the acute phase of myocardial infarction, ischaemia creates electrical heterogeneity that favours polymorphic VT and VF, whereas monomorphic VT usually reflects re-entry around an old scar. Once ischaemia is excluded, other causes of polymorphic VT with a normal QT include cardiomyopathies, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, Brugada syndrome, short QT syndrome, malignant early repolarisation and short-coupled torsades. Investigations then include imaging (echocardiography, MRI), exercise testing, drug challenge and genetic testing as appropriate.

ecg-tachy-058.question: An 11-year-old boy has syncope during a football match. Resting ECG is normal (QTc 420 ms). On exercise testing: polymorphic PVCs, then bidirectional VT above 120 bpm. Which diagnosis should be considered?
options: Brugada syndrome with an intermittent ECG pattern
commentaires: Incorrect: events in Brugada syndrome occur mainly at rest or at night, not on exercise.
Incorrect: the QTc is normal, and LQT3 causes events at rest or during sleep.
Incorrect: outflow tract VT is monomorphic; bidirectional VT suggests CPVT or digoxin toxicity.
Correct: normal resting ECG, increasingly complex PVCs then bidirectional VT on exercise: CPVT.
ecg-tachy-058.explication: CPVT is a channelopathy (most often an RYR2 mutation, dominant inheritance) with a normal resting ECG, presenting with syncope or sudden cardiac death during exercise or emotional stress in children and young adults. The exercise test is the key investigation: above a threshold heart rate, increasingly complex PVCs appear, progressing to bidirectional VT (alternating QRS axis) or polymorphic VT. The other causes of bidirectional VT are digitalis toxicity and Andersen–Tawil syndrome. Treatment is based on non-selective beta-blockers (nadolol), flecainide and, if needed, left cardiac sympathetic denervation.
ecg-tachy-058.aRetenir: Exercise-induced bidirectional VT in a child with a normal ECG = CPVT.
ecg-tachy-058.rappel: CPVT is caused by diastolic calcium leak from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (ryanodine receptor RYR2, dominant form; calsequestrin CASQ2, recessive form), generating delayed afterdepolarisations under adrenergic stimulation. All diagnosed patients should receive a non-selective beta-blocker and avoid strenuous exercise; flecainide is added if arrhythmias persist. The ICD is reserved for resuscitated or refractory patients, because painful shocks can trigger an electrical storm; it must be programmed with long detection times. Family screening (exercise testing, genetics) is essential.

ecg-tachy-059.question: An unconscious patient has no pulse; the monitor shows this tracing. What are the diagnosis and the priority action?
options: Artefact: check the electrodes and wait
commentaires: Incorrect: asystole is a flat line; here the activity is chaotic and of large amplitude.
Incorrect: torsades retain organised complexes in spindles; here no QRS is identifiable.
Correct: chaotic activity with no QRS in a pulseless patient: immediate defibrillation and CPR.
Incorrect: an unconscious, pulseless patient requires action without delay.
ecg-tachy-059.explication: On this tracing the electrical activity is chaotic, with no organised complexes: in a pulseless patient this is ventricular fibrillation. It is a "shockable" rhythm: treatment is immediate defibrillation (unsynchronised shock) combined with cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Every minute of delay reduces the probability of survival. Asystole is a flat line. Torsades de pointes retain organised complexes in spindles. Artefact should be considered if the patient is conscious, but here the absence of a pulse requires action without delay.
ecg-tachy-059.rappel: In cardiac arrest, rhythms are divided into shockable (VF, pulseless VT) and non-shockable (asystole, pulseless electrical activity). VF may be coarse or fine, the latter mimicking asystole: check the gain and several leads. Interruptions in chest compressions must be minimised, including around shocks. In refractory VF, adrenaline and amiodarone are added according to resuscitation guidelines. After VF without an acute reversible cause, an ICD is indicated for secondary prevention.

ecg-tachy-060.question: With this tracing in a pulseless patient, the shock delivered must be synchronised to the QRS.
commentaires: Incorrect: in VF there is no organised QRS; a synchronised shock would never be delivered.
Correct: VF is defibrillated with an unsynchronised shock; synchronisation is reserved for organised tachycardias with a pulse.
ecg-tachy-060.explication: False. This tracing shows ventricular fibrillation: there is no organised QRS on which to synchronise the shock, and the defibrillator would never discharge. The defibrillation shock is therefore unsynchronised. Synchronisation is, by contrast, essential for cardioversion of organised tachycardias (AF, flutter, VT with a pulse), to avoid delivering the shock during the vulnerable phase of the T wave and inducing VF. Pulseless VT is treated like VF.
ecg-tachy-060.aRetenir: VF and pulseless VT: unsynchronised shock; organised tachycardias with a pulse: synchronised shock.
ecg-tachy-060.rappel: Defibrillation simultaneously depolarises a critical mass of myocardium, which interrupts the multiple re-entrant wavefronts of VF and allows the sinus node to regain control. Biphasic waveforms are more effective than monophasic ones at lower energy. Pads are placed in the anterolateral or anteroposterior position, away from the can of a pacemaker or ICD, whose function must be checked after the shock. After each shock, chest compressions resume immediately, without a pulse check, for two minutes before the next rhythm analysis.

ecg-tachy-061.question: A 60-year-old man has a radial pulse of 38 bpm, whereas the monitor displays 76 bpm. How should the rhythm on this tracing be described?
options: 2:1 AV block with bundle branch block
commentaires: Incorrect: no premature P wave precedes the wide complexes.
Correct: each sinus QRS is followed by a wide PVC with no P wave; the haemodynamically ineffective PVCs explain the pulse deficit.
Incorrect: the wide complexes are premature and are not preceded by any conducted P wave.
Incorrect: at least 3 consecutive ventricular complexes are needed; here they alternate with sinus beats.
ecg-tachy-061.explication: On this tracing each narrow sinus QRS is followed by a wide, premature QRS not preceded by a P wave. A premature ventricular contraction is a premature, wide (> 120 ms) QRS, differing in morphology from the baseline QRS, not preceded by a premature P wave, with a T wave of opposite polarity. When every sinus beat is followed by a PVC, this is ventricular bigeminy. Atrial bigeminy consists of premature complexes preceded by a premature P wave, usually with narrow QRS complexes. Non-sustained VT requires at least 3 consecutive ventricular complexes. The palpated pulse is falsely low here, because early PVCs are haemodynamically ineffective.
ecg-tachy-061.aRetenir: A PVC after every sinus QRS = ventricular bigeminy.
ecg-tachy-061.rappel: PVCs are described by their morphology (monomorphic or polymorphic), coupling interval and grouping: bigeminy (one PVC after each sinus beat), trigeminy (one PVC after every two sinus beats), couplet (two consecutive PVCs); from three onwards, the term non-sustained VT is used. Monomorphic PVCs with a fixed coupling interval generally reflect re-entry or triggered activity linked to the preceding beat. A variable coupling interval, with inter-ectopic intervals that are multiples of a common cycle and fusion beats, suggests parasystole, a protected focus firing at its own rate.

ecg-tachy-062.question: A 50-year-old woman reports a sensation of "thumps" in her chest. How should the premature beats on this tracing be interpreted?
commentaires: Correct: premature P wave of different morphology, followed by a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS.
Incorrect: a PVC would be wide, with no premature P wave.
Incorrect: a capture beat is only meaningful during ventricular tachycardia or AV dissociation.
Incorrect: an escape beat occurs late, after a pause; these beats are premature.
ecg-tachy-062.explication: On this tracing the premature beats have a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS and are preceded by a P wave of different morphology. A premature atrial contraction is recognised by a premature P wave whose morphology differs from the sinus P wave (because it arises elsewhere in the atrium), usually followed by a narrow QRS identical to the baseline QRS. The ensuing pause is usually non-compensatory, because the PAC penetrates and "resets" the sinus node. A PVC is wide, with no premature P wave. An escape beat is late, not premature. A very early PAC may be blocked (no QRS) or conducted with aberrancy (wide QRS), two common pitfalls.
ecg-tachy-062.aRetenir: PAC = premature P wave of different morphology, usually a narrow QRS.
ecg-tachy-062.rappel: Narrow-QRS premature beats are atrial or junctional. The P' wave of a PAC has a morphology that depends on its origin: close to the sinus P wave for a high right atrial origin, negative in the inferior leads for a low origin, and its PR interval is usually ≥ 120 ms. A premature junctional beat arises from the AV node or His bundle: it comes with a retrograde P wave, negative in the inferior leads, just before the QRS with a short PR interval (< 120 ms), hidden within the QRS or just after it. The earlier a PAC, the longer its PR interval (decremental AV nodal conduction).

ecg-tachy-063.question: Why is a premature ventricular contraction classically followed by a fully compensatory pause?
options: It resets the sinus node retrogradely
It causes transient complete AV block
It transiently blocks the right bundle branch
It does not reset the sinus node
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the mechanism of a PAC, which explains its non-compensatory pause.
Incorrect: the non-conducted P wave is blocked by physiological refractoriness, not by pathological AV block.
Incorrect: the compensatory pause does not depend on bundle branch block.
Correct: the sinus node continues at its own rate; the next P wave, falling in the refractory period, is not conducted: exactly 2 cycles.
ecg-tachy-063.explication: A PVC is not usually conducted retrogradely as far as the sinus node, which continues to fire at its own rate. The sinus P wave occurring during or just after the PVC finds the AV node or the ventricles refractory and is not conducted; the next sinus beat therefore arrives on time. The interval between the QRS preceding and the QRS following the PVC is then exactly two sinus cycles: this is the fully compensatory pause. A PAC usually resets the sinus node, hence a non-compensatory pause. A PVC can also be interpolated (with no pause) when the sinus rate is slow.
ecg-tachy-063.aRetenir: PVC: fully compensatory pause (2 sinus cycles); PAC: non-compensatory pause.
ecg-tachy-063.rappel: The behaviour of the pause after a PVC depends on retrograde conduction and sinus rate. An interpolated PVC, with no pause, occurs between two sinus beats when the rate is slow; its concealed retrograde penetration into the AV node often prolongs the PR interval of the next sinus beat. If the PVC is conducted retrogradely to the atria and resets the sinus node, the pause becomes non-compensatory. Conversely, a PAC may produce a compensatory pause if it does not penetrate the sinus node. The type of pause is therefore a clue, not proof of origin.

ecg-tachy-064.question: A Holter recording shows several pauses with no QRS. On close inspection, the T wave preceding each pause is deformed (notched) compared with the other T waves. What is the most likely explanation?
commentaires: Correct: the premature, non-conducted P wave is superimposed on the preceding T wave, which it deforms.
Incorrect: a sinus pause is not accompanied by deformation of the preceding T wave.
Incorrect: in Mobitz II the blocked P wave occurs on time and remains visible; it does not deform the T wave.
Incorrect: no pacemaker is mentioned; the deformed T wave indicates a premature P wave.
ecg-tachy-064.explication: A very early PAC can occur while the AV node is still refractory: it is not conducted to the ventricles. Its premature P wave is superimposed on the preceding T wave, which it deforms. The ensuing pause is often mistaken for a sinus pause or AV block. A blocked PAC is the most common cause of an unexplained pause on a Holter recording. In Mobitz II, blocked P waves occur on time (constant PP interval), not prematurely. Comparing T-wave morphology should become routine whenever a pause is seen.
ecg-tachy-064.aRetenir: Pause preceded by a deformed T wave = blocked PAC.
ecg-tachy-064.rappel: When faced with a pause, analysis of the P waves distinguishes four mechanisms. Sinus pause: no P wave, with a duration unrelated to the baseline cycle. SA block: a pause equal to a multiple of the PP interval. AV block: a P wave on time, not followed by a QRS. Blocked PAC: a premature P wave, often hidden in the T wave. Blocked atrial bigeminy can mimic regular sinus bradycardia, with a ventricular rate half the true atrial rate. On Holter recordings, artefact or signal loss must also be excluded.

ecg-tachy-065.question: Ashman phenomenon is the aberrant conduction, usually with an RBBB-like pattern, of a supraventricular complex occurring after a long–short cycle sequence.
commentaires: Correct: the refractory period depends on the preceding cycle; after a long cycle, an early complex finds the right bundle branch refractory.
Incorrect: the statement is true; it is a classic cause of a wide complex wrongly taken for a PVC in AF.
ecg-tachy-065.explication: The refractory period of the His–Purkinje system depends on the length of the preceding cycle: the longer the preceding cycle, the longer the subsequent refractory period. A premature complex following a long cycle may therefore find a bundle branch still refractory, most often the right bundle branch (which has the longest refractory period), hence an RBBB-like pattern. This phenomenon is common in AF, where it is often wrongly taken for PVCs. The absence of a compensatory pause and a typical bundle branch block morphology favour aberrancy.
ecg-tachy-065.aRetenir: Ashman: long then short cycle → aberrant complex (RBBB-like), not to be mistaken for a PVC.
ecg-tachy-065.rappel: In AF, distinguishing an aberrant complex from a PVC relies on several clues. Favouring aberrancy: typical bundle branch block morphology (often rsR' in V1), an initial vector identical to the conducted QRS complexes, a variable coupling interval and no prolonged pause after the complex. Favouring a PVC: a fixed coupling interval, atypical morphology and a longer pause after the complex (concealed retrograde penetration into the AV node). A long–short cycle sequence is common in AF and is therefore not, on its own, proof of aberrancy.

ecg-tachy-066.question: A patient has an unexplained LVEF of 35% (normal coronary arteries, no late gadolinium enhancement on MRI) and monomorphic PVCs on Holter. According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, above which burden should PVC-induced cardiomyopathy be suspected?
commentaires: Incorrect: a 1% burden does not explain LV dysfunction.
Incorrect: a 5% burden is rarely sufficient to explain LV dysfunction.
Correct: ESC 2022 advises suspecting PVC-induced cardiomyopathy from a burden of 10% (class IIa).
Incorrect: far too high a threshold; the risk appears from 10%, often > 20% in published series.
ecg-tachy-066.explication: The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend that PVC-induced cardiomyopathy be suspected in a patient with unexplained LV dysfunction and a PVC burden of at least 10% of beats (class IIa). The risk increases with burden (often > 20% in published series), but also with PVC width, epicardial origin and interpolation. The diagnosis is confirmed retrospectively by improvement in LVEF after PVC suppression (first-line ablation or antiarrhythmic drug). A burden of 1 to 5% is rarely sufficient to explain LV dysfunction.
ecg-tachy-066.aRetenir: Unexplained LV dysfunction + PVCs ≥ 10%: think arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy and consider ablation.
ecg-tachy-066.rappel: PVC burden is expressed as a percentage of the total number of beats recorded. It varies from day to day, so a 24-hour Holter may underestimate it; a multi-day recording is more representative. PVC-induced cardiomyopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion, which justifies a search for underlying heart disease (MRI, coronary assessment). PVCs can also worsen a pre-existing cardiomyopathy and reduce the percentage of biventricular pacing in a patient with CRT. Suppression of PVCs, by ablation or antiarrhythmic drugs, aims at recovery of LVEF.

ecg-tachy-067.question: Which ECG appearance defines the type 1 Brugada pattern?
options: Saddleback ST elevation ≥ 2 mm with a positive T in V1–V2
Epsilon wave and negative T waves in V1–V3
Coved ST elevation ≥ 2 mm with a negative T in V1 or V2
Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
commentaires: Incorrect: this is type 2 (saddleback), which is only suggestive and requires a search for a type 1 pattern.
Incorrect: an epsilon wave and negative T waves in V1–V3 suggest arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.
Correct: convex, downsloping ST elevation ≥ 2 mm followed by a negative T wave in V1 and/or V2: the only diagnostic pattern.
Incorrect: this picture suggests acute pericarditis.
ecg-tachy-067.explication: The type 1 Brugada pattern combines, in V1 and/or V2 (recorded in the 2nd, 3rd or 4th intercostal spaces), J-point/ST elevation ≥ 2 mm that is downsloping and convex ("coved"), followed by a negative T wave. It is the only diagnostic pattern. Type 2 (saddleback) is merely suggestive and requires a drug challenge to unmask a type 1 pattern. An epsilon wave is a sign of ARVC. Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression suggests pericarditis. Recording V1–V2 in a high position increases sensitivity.
ecg-tachy-067.aRetenir: Type 1 Brugada: coved ST ≥ 2 mm + negative T in V1–V2 (including high-placed leads).
ecg-tachy-067.rappel: The Brugada pattern fluctuates: it may be spontaneously present, intermittent or absent from one day to the next, hence the value of repeated ECGs and recordings in high positions (2nd and 3rd intercostal spaces), which better overlie the RV outflow tract. Type 2, the saddleback pattern, has ST elevation with an upward concavity and a positive or flat T wave. Several conditions mimic a Brugada pattern: RBBB, athlete's repolarisation, pectus excavatum, arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy, and "phenocopies" (metabolic disturbances, ischaemia, mediastinal compression), which resolve with the cause.

ecg-tachy-068.question: Which factors can unmask or aggravate a type 1 Brugada pattern?
commentaires: Correct: fever further reduces the sodium current; it must be treated promptly in these patients.
Correct: used as a diagnostic challenge to unmask a type 1 pattern.
Incorrect: isoprenaline is used to treat electrical storm in Brugada syndrome.
Incorrect: quinidine (an Ito blocker) is a treatment for Brugada syndrome.
ecg-tachy-068.explication: Brugada syndrome is most often related to a reduced sodium current (SCN5A). Anything that further reduces this current accentuates the ECG pattern and the arrhythmic risk: fever (so much so that fever must be treated promptly in these patients), sodium channel blockers (used as a diagnostic challenge: ajmaline, flecainide), certain psychotropic drugs, anaesthetic agents, alcohol and cocaine. Vagal tone (rest, sleep, large meals) also accentuates the pattern. Conversely, isoprenaline and quinidine (which blocks the Ito current) are used to treat electrical storm. The list of drugs to avoid is kept up to date on dedicated databases.
ecg-tachy-068.aRetenir: Brugada: fever and sodium channel blockers unmask; isoprenaline and quinidine treat.
ecg-tachy-068.rappel: Brugada syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, with a clear male predominance; an SCN5A mutation is found in only a minority of patients. The substrate lies in the epicardium of the RV outflow tract, where the transient outward potassium current Ito is prominent: the imbalance between inward and outward currents early in repolarisation, together with local conduction delay, explains the ECG pattern and the arrhythmias. Events occur mainly at rest and at night, under vagal influence. A list of drugs to avoid is kept up to date on a dedicated website (brugadadrugs.org).

ecg-tachy-069.question: According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, a spontaneous type 2 ("saddleback") Brugada pattern is sufficient to diagnose Brugada syndrome.
commentaires: Incorrect: only the type 1 pattern, spontaneous or unmasked, is diagnostic.
Correct: a type 2 pattern should prompt a search for a type 1 pattern (high lead placement, drug challenge, ECG during fever).
ecg-tachy-069.explication: Only the type 1 pattern, spontaneous or unmasked, is diagnostic. A type 2 pattern should prompt a search for a type 1 pattern (high lead placement, ajmaline or flecainide challenge, ECG during fever). According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, a spontaneous type 1 pattern is sufficient for the diagnosis in the absence of other heart disease. By contrast, a type 1 pattern induced only by a sodium channel blocker requires at least one additional feature (arrhythmic syncope or nocturnal agonal respiration, family history of Brugada syndrome or of sudden death at a young age with a negative autopsy). This limits false positives related to the drug challenge.
ecg-tachy-069.aRetenir: Brugada: only type 1 is diagnostic; an induced type 1 pattern requires an additional clinical criterion.
ecg-tachy-069.rappel: Management of Brugada syndrome is based on arrhythmic risk. According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, an ICD is recommended (class I) after resuscitated cardiac arrest or documented sustained VT, and should be considered (class IIa) in patients with arrhythmic syncope and a spontaneous type 1 pattern. All patients should avoid contraindicated drugs, excessive alcohol and large meals, and treat any fever promptly. In patients receiving recurrent shocks, quinidine or ablation of the epicardial substrate in the RV outflow tract are options.

ecg-tachy-070.question: Measured QT 400 ms, RR interval 640 ms (HR ≈ 94 bpm). What is the QTc according to Bazett?
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the raw, uncorrected QT.
Incorrect: this value does not correspond to any standard formula; Fridericia would give about 465 ms.
Incorrect: the classic error of dividing by the RR (400/0.64) instead of by its square root.
ecg-tachy-070.explication: The Bazett formula is QTc = QT / √RR (RR in seconds). Here √0.64 = 0.8, so QTc = 400 / 0.8 = 500 ms, which is clearly prolonged. The classic error is to divide by the RR rather than by its square root (400/0.64 = 625 ms). Bazett, however, overcorrects at high heart rates: at 94 bpm the value obtained may overestimate the QTc, and the Fridericia formula (cube root) gives about 465 ms here. A borderline QTc at a fast rate should therefore be interpreted with caution and, if possible, rechecked at a slower rate.
ecg-tachy-070.aRetenir: Bazett: QTc = QT/√RR (in seconds); beware of overcorrection during tachycardia.
ecg-tachy-070.rappel: The QT interval shortens as heart rate increases, hence the need for correction. Bazett divides by the square root of the RR interval, Fridericia by its cube root; linear formulas (Framingham, Hodges) perform better at extreme rates, and the AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations encourage linear correction. According to these recommendations, a QTc is considered prolonged from 450 ms in men and 460 ms in women, and short at 390 ms or less. In AF, the QT interval should be averaged over several cycles, as the RR interval varies from beat to beat.

ecg-tachy-071.question: Why is the Fridericia formula often preferred to Bazett in a tachycardic patient (e.g. in fast AF or on a drug that can cause torsades)?
options: Bazett undercorrects the QTc at high heart rates
Bazett overcorrects the QTc at high heart rates
Fridericia is the only formula validated in women
Fridericia does not require the RR to be measured
commentaires: Incorrect: it is the opposite; Bazett undercorrects at slow heart rates.
Correct: during tachycardia, Bazett overestimates the QTc and can lead to a wrong conclusion of long QT.
Incorrect: no formula has this status; the choice is driven by rate dependence.
Incorrect: all correction formulae require measurement of the RR.
ecg-tachy-071.explication: The Bazett correction (QT/√RR) excessively lengthens the QTc at high heart rates and shortens it at slow rates. During tachycardia it can therefore lead to a wrong conclusion of long QT, resulting in unnecessary discontinuation of treatment. The Fridericia formula (QT/∛RR) and linear formulae (Framingham, Hodges) are less rate-dependent. The AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations on ECG standardisation highlight these limitations and advise using a linear correction. All formulae require measurement of the RR.
ecg-tachy-071.aRetenir: Bazett overcorrects during tachycardia: prefer Fridericia or a linear formula.
ecg-tachy-071.rappel: Measuring the QT interval requires a few precautions. Automatic values from ECG machines are often wrong (flat T wave, U wave, artefacts) and must be checked manually. In AF the RR interval varies: QT and RR are averaged over several cycles rather than correcting a single beat. When the QRS is wide (bundle branch block, ventricular pacing), part of the QT prolongation reflects depolarisation only: the JT interval is then more relevant. Finally, a borderline value obtained during tachycardia should be rechecked at a slower rate before changing treatment.

ecg-tachy-072.question: Congenital long QT: bifid, low-amplitude T wave, with syncopal episodes triggered by an alarm clock. Which genotype is most likely?
commentaires: Incorrect: LQT1 produces a broad T wave and events on exertion, particularly swimming.
Incorrect: LQT3 produces a long isoelectric ST segment and events at rest or during sleep.
Incorrect: a recessive form with congenital deafness, not suggested here.
Correct: low-amplitude, bifid T waves and events triggered by sudden auditory stimuli.
ecg-tachy-072.explication: The three main genotypes have fairly typical profiles. LQT2 (KCNH2, IKr current) produces low-amplitude, bifid or notched T waves, with events triggered by sudden auditory stimuli (alarm clock, telephone) or in the postpartum period. LQT1 (KCNQ1, IKs) produces a broad-based T wave, with events on exertion, particularly swimming. LQT3 (SCN5A, late sodium current) combines a long isoelectric ST segment followed by a late T wave, with events at rest or during sleep. Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is a recessive form with congenital deafness.
ecg-tachy-072.aRetenir: LQT1: exertion/swimming; LQT2: bifid T, auditory stimuli; LQT3: rest/sleep.
ecg-tachy-072.rappel: Congenital long QT syndrome most often results from loss of function of the repolarising potassium currents (IKs in LQT1, IKr in LQT2) or gain of function of the late sodium current (LQT3). Heterogeneous prolongation of the action potential favours early afterdepolarisations and torsades de pointes. Basic treatment is a non-selective beta-blocker (nadolol, propranolol) for all patients with a prolonged QT interval, together with avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs and correction of any hypokalaemia. Mexiletine, a late sodium current blocker, is an option in LQT3.

ecg-tachy-073.question: A teenager has a syncopal episode and narrowly escapes drowning during a swimming session. His ECG shows a QTc of 490 ms with broad T waves. Which genotype is most likely?
commentaires: Incorrect: LQT2 events are typically triggered by sudden auditory stimuli.
Correct: swimming and exertion are the classic triggers of LQT1, with broad T waves.
Incorrect: LQT3 causes events at rest or during sleep.
Incorrect: Brugada syndrome is not associated with a long QT, and its events occur mainly at rest.
ecg-tachy-073.explication: Swimming and physical exertion are the classic triggers of LQT1, the most common form of congenital long QT. Loss of function of the IKs current prevents appropriate QT shortening during adrenergic stimulation. Beta-blockers (nadolol, propranolol) are particularly effective in this genotype. LQT2 events are typically triggered by auditory stimuli and LQT3 events occur at rest. Brugada syndrome is not associated with a long QT and its events occur mainly at rest or at night.
ecg-tachy-073.rappel: In congenital long QT syndrome, the risk of events increases with QTc duration (particularly above 500 ms) and a history of syncope or cardiac arrest, and varies with genotype, sex and age. LQT1, due to KCNQ1, is expressed mainly during adrenergic stimulation, hence avoidance of strenuous exercise, particularly competitive swimming. Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome, a recessive homozygous or compound heterozygous form involving KCNQ1 or KCNE1, combines congenital deafness with a very high arrhythmic risk. Relatives should undergo an ECG and cascade genetic testing.

ecg-tachy-074.question: In the Schwartz score (congenital long QT), which QTc value measured at the 4th minute of recovery after an exercise test scores 1 point?
ecg-tachy-074.reponseAttendue: QTc ≥ 480 ms at the 4th minute of recovery.
ecg-tachy-074.explication: In healthy individuals, the QT shortens on exercise and remains appropriately adapted during recovery. In patients with long QT, particularly LQT1, the QTc does not shorten normally and remains prolonged during recovery. Schwartz and Crotti added this criterion to the diagnostic score in 2011: a QTc ≥ 480 ms at the 4th minute of recovery scores 1 point. The exercise test is therefore a useful tool in patients whose resting QTc is borderline. The Schwartz score is still used in the 2022 ESC guidelines (diagnosis established if the score is > 3).
ecg-tachy-074.aRetenir: QTc ≥ 480 ms at the 4th minute of recovery = 1 point in the Schwartz score.
ecg-tachy-074.rappel: The Schwartz score combines ECG, clinical and family criteria. ECG criteria: QTc ≥ 480 ms (3 points), 460–479 ms (2 points), 450–459 ms in men (1 point), torsades de pointes (2 points), T-wave alternans (1 point), notched T waves in three leads (1 point), low heart rate for age (0.5 point). Clinical criteria: syncope with exertion or stress (2 points), without stress (1 point), congenital deafness (0.5 point). Family criteria: definite long QT syndrome (1 point), unexplained sudden cardiac death before age 30 in a first-degree relative (0.5 point). A score ≥ 3.5 indicates a high probability.

ecg-tachy-075.question: A 24-year-old man has paroxysmal AF and a family history of sudden cardiac death. ECG: QTc 320 ms, almost absent ST segment, tall peaked T waves, QT varying little with heart rate. Which diagnosis should be suspected?
commentaires: Incorrect: hyperkalaemia also produces peaked T waves, but in a suggestive context (renal failure).
Incorrect: early repolarisation does not shorten the QT.
Correct: QTc ≤ 320 ms, almost absent ST segment, tall peaked T waves, AF at a young age and family history of sudden death.
Incorrect: hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT (long ST segment).
ecg-tachy-075.explication: Short QT syndrome combines a short QTc, an almost absent ST segment with tall, peaked, symmetrical T waves, and poor QT adaptation to heart rate. According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, the diagnosis is established for a QTc ≤ 360 ms combined with a pathogenic mutation, a family history of short QT or resuscitated VT/VF in a structurally normal heart (class I); it should be considered with an isolated QTc ≤ 320 ms (class IIa) and may be considered between 320 and 360 ms with arrhythmic syncope (class IIb). This patient (QTc 320 ms, AF at a young age, family history of sudden death) therefore meets these criteria. Secondary causes of short QT must be excluded (hypercalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperthermia, acidosis, digoxin). Hyperkalaemia also produces peaked T waves, but in a suggestive context (renal failure) and, at advanced stages, with flattened P waves and QRS widening. Early repolarisation does not shorten the QT, and hypocalcaemia prolongs it (long ST segment).
ecg-tachy-075.aRetenir: Short QT (ESC 2022): QTc ≤ 320 ms, or ≤ 360 ms with a mutation, family history or resuscitated VT/VF; tall peaked T waves, AF at a young age.
ecg-tachy-075.rappel: Short QT syndrome is due to gain-of-function mutations in potassium channels (notably KCNH2, KCNQ1, KCNJ2) that shorten the action potential and the atrial and ventricular refractory periods, favouring both AF and VF. It may present in childhood, with a high risk of sudden cardiac death. According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, an ICD is recommended (class I) after resuscitated cardiac arrest or documented sustained VT. Quinidine, which prolongs the QT interval, is a pharmacological option. At EP study, refractory periods are short and VF is often inducible.

ecg-tachy-076.question: According to the 2015 consensus, how is the early repolarisation pattern defined?
options: J point ≥ 0.1 mV with notch or slur in inferior/lateral leads
Coved ST elevation ≥ 2 mm followed by a negative T wave in V1–V3
Diffuse ST depression with a prominent U wave and flattened T waves
J point ≥ 0.1 mV with a notch confined to leads V1–V3
commentaires: Correct: terminal notch or slur with a J point ≥ 0.1 mV in at least 2 contiguous inferior and/or lateral leads.
Incorrect: this is the type 1 Brugada pattern.
Incorrect: ST depression and a U wave suggest hypokalaemia.
Incorrect: leads V1–V3 are excluded from the definition, as they belong to the Brugada domain.
ecg-tachy-076.explication: The early repolarisation pattern is defined by a J wave (notch) or slur on the terminal downslope of a prominent R wave, with a J-point peak ≥ 0.1 mV in at least two contiguous leads of the 12-lead ECG, excluding V1 to V3, and a QRS < 120 ms. Leads V1–V3 are excluded as they belong to the Brugada domain. This pattern is common in young people and athletes and is generally benign. The profiles associated with higher risk are an amplitude ≥ 2 mm, an inferior or diffuse location, and a horizontal or descending ST segment.
ecg-tachy-076.aRetenir: Early repolarisation: J point ≥ 1 mm with notch/slur in ≥ 2 contiguous inferior/lateral leads (excluding V1–V3).
ecg-tachy-076.rappel: The J wave of early repolarisation reflects a transmural voltage gradient early in repolarisation, due to the transient outward potassium current Ito, which is larger in the epicardium than in the endocardium. The pattern is accentuated by vagal tone and bradycardia, and attenuated by faster heart rates; an increase in J waves after a pause may precede VF in at-risk individuals. A "notch" is a distinct positive J wave at the end of the QRS, a "slur" a smooth transition in the downstroke of the R wave. Osborn J waves in hypothermia share a similar mechanism and are a differential diagnosis.

ecg-tachy-077.question: Incidental discovery of an inferolateral early repolarisation pattern in an asymptomatic individual with no family history warrants ICD implantation.
commentaires: Incorrect: the isolated pattern is common and overwhelmingly benign; there is no indication for an ICD.
Correct: early repolarisation syndrome is reserved for survivors of unexplained VF; the isolated pattern does not warrant an ICD.
ecg-tachy-077.explication: The early repolarisation pattern is found in about 5 to 10% of the general population, more often in young people and athletes, and is overwhelmingly benign. Haïssaguerre showed its higher prevalence among survivors of idiopathic VF, but the absolute risk in an asymptomatic individual remains very low. The 2022 ESC guidelines reserve the diagnosis of early repolarisation syndrome for survivors of unexplained VF with this pattern and do not recommend routine investigation in asymptomatic individuals; there is no indication for an ICD with an isolated pattern. It should therefore be neither over-investigated nor labelled as pathological.
ecg-tachy-077.aRetenir: Isolated asymptomatic early repolarisation: a benign pattern, no ICD.
ecg-tachy-077.rappel: Early repolarisation syndrome is diagnosed in a survivor of unexplained VF, after a complete work-up excluding structural heart disease, ischaemia and other channelopathies, in the presence of an early repolarisation pattern. An ICD is then indicated for secondary prevention. During an electrical storm, isoprenaline, which increases heart rate and reduces J waves, can suppress recurrences; quinidine is used for prevention. In relatives, finding an isolated pattern is not enough to define individual risk, and no preventive treatment is offered to asymptomatic individuals.

ecg-tachy-078.question: What does the epsilon wave, an ECG sign of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, look like?
options: A small positive wave following the T wave in V2–V3
A broad, deep Q wave in II, III and aVF
Notching of the initial part of the QRS in V1–V3
A small late signal after the QRS in V1–V3
commentaires: Incorrect: a positive wave after the T wave is a U wave, not an epsilon wave.
Incorrect: inferior Q waves suggest a previous myocardial infarction.
Incorrect: initial QRS notching suggests a delta wave; the epsilon wave is terminal.
Correct: a reproducible low-amplitude signal between the end of the QRS and the onset of the T wave: delayed RV activation.
ecg-tachy-078.explication: The epsilon wave is a small, reproducible, low-amplitude signal located between the end of the QRS and the onset of the T wave in the right precordial leads (V1 to V3). It reflects delayed activation of RV regions replaced by fibrofatty tissue. In the 2010 Task Force criteria, it is a major depolarisation criterion. It is best seen with appropriate filtering, amplification and a faster paper speed. It must be distinguished from simple notching or artefact, which explains substantial inter-observer variability. A wave located after the T wave is a U wave, and initial QRS notching suggests a delta wave (pre-excitation).
ecg-tachy-078.aRetenir: Epsilon wave: a late low-amplitude signal after the QRS in V1–V3, a major criterion for ARVC.
ecg-tachy-078.rappel: The epsilon wave, of very low amplitude, is easily masked by restrictive low-pass filtering on the ECG machine (such as 40 Hz): a wide filter setting, doubled gain and a faster paper speed help to identify it. Dedicated bipolar leads (Fontaine leads) also improve its detection. It is not entirely specific: it may be seen in other RV diseases (notably cardiac sarcoidosis). The other depolarisation abnormalities in arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy, which are minor criteria, are late potentials on the signal-averaged ECG and prolonged terminal activation duration in V1–V3.

ecg-tachy-079.question: According to the 2010 Task Force criteria for ARVC, which ECG signs are MAJOR criteria?
options: Inverted T waves in V1, V2, V3 (or beyond) in individuals over 14 years without complete RBBB
Epsilon wave in the right precordial leads
Inverted T waves confined to V1–V2
Terminal activation duration of QRS ≥ 55 ms in V1–V3
commentaires: Correct: a major repolarisation criterion in the 2010 Task Force criteria.
Correct: a major depolarisation criterion.
Incorrect: inverted T waves confined to V1–V2 are a minor criterion.
Incorrect: a prolonged terminal activation duration is a minor criterion.
ecg-tachy-079.explication: In the 2010 Task Force criteria, the major repolarisation abnormalities are inverted T waves in V1, V2 and V3 or beyond, in individuals over 14 years of age, in the absence of complete right bundle branch block (QRS ≥ 120 ms). The major depolarisation criterion is the epsilon wave in V1–V3. Inverted T waves confined to V1–V2 are a minor criterion. A terminal activation duration ≥ 55 ms (from the nadir of the S wave to the end of the QRS) in V1–V3 and late potentials are also minor criteria. The diagnosis also incorporates imaging, histology, arrhythmias and family/genetic history.
ecg-tachy-079.aRetenir: ARVC (2010 TFC): inverted T waves in V1–V3 and epsilon wave = major ECG criteria.
ecg-tachy-079.rappel: The 2010 Task Force criteria fall into six categories: structural and functional RV abnormalities, tissue characterisation (biopsy), repolarisation, depolarisation, arrhythmias, and family history and genetics. The diagnosis is definite with 2 major criteria, 1 major plus 2 minor, or 4 minor criteria from different categories; borderline with 1 major plus 1 minor, or 3 minor; possible with 1 major or 2 minor. Minor repolarisation criteria also include T-wave inversion in V4–V6, and T-wave inversion in V1 to V4 in the presence of complete RBBB.

ecg-tachy-080.question: What is the first ECG abnormality expected in moderate hyperkalaemia?
commentaires: Incorrect: apparent QT prolongation (in fact QU) is a sign of hypokalaemia.
Incorrect: a prominent U wave is a sign of hypokalaemia.
Correct: accelerated repolarisation produces tall, peaked, symmetrical T waves from 5.5 to 6.5 mmol/l.
Incorrect: ST depression is a sign of hypokalaemia.
ecg-tachy-080.explication: Hyperkalaemia accelerates repolarisation, producing tall, peaked, narrow-based, symmetrical ("tented") T waves, typically visible from 5.5–6.5 mmol/l. As it worsens, flattening of the P waves, PR prolongation and QRS widening appear, followed finally by a sine-wave pattern preceding VF or asystole. The correlation between serum potassium and the ECG is, however, imperfect: a near-normal ECG is not reassuring. The U wave, ST depression and QT (in fact QU) prolongation are signs of hypokalaemia.
ecg-tachy-080.aRetenir: Hyperkalaemia: tall peaked T waves first, then flattened P waves, wide QRS, sine wave.
ecg-tachy-080.rappel: Hyperkalaemia increases potassium conductance, which accelerates phase 3 repolarisation (peaked T waves), and partially depolarises the resting membrane, reducing sodium channel availability and slowing conduction (flattened P waves, prolonged PR and QRS). Severity depends as much on the speed of onset as on the level. The main causes are renal failure, drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, potassium-sparing diuretics), acidosis and cell lysis. Haemolysis of the sample causes pseudohyperkalaemia: a normal ECG should raise this possibility, without dispensing with a prompt repeat test.

ecg-tachy-081.question: A dialysis patient has missed two sessions. ECG: regular rhythm at 40 bpm, QRS 200 ms, no visible P waves, incipient sine-wave pattern. What is the first treatment to give?
options: IV isoprenaline as a continuous infusion
IV amiodarone for presumed slow VT
commentaires: Incorrect: isoprenaline does not treat the cause and does not stabilise the myocardial membrane.
Correct: calcium stabilises the membrane within minutes, before insulin–glucose and dialysis.
Incorrect: this is not VT; amiodarone is useless and dangerous here.
Incorrect: capture may fail because of raised thresholds; calcium comes first.
ecg-tachy-081.explication: In a dialysis patient who has missed sessions, a slow rhythm with very wide QRS complexes and no visible P waves suggests severe hyperkalaemia. It must not be mistaken for slow VT or simple AV block. The first treatment is IV calcium, which stabilises the myocardial membrane within minutes without lowering serum potassium. This is combined with insulin–glucose and beta-2 agonists (intracellular potassium shift), followed by potassium removal (emergency dialysis). Amiodarone is useless and dangerous. Cardiac pacing may fail because of the rise in pacing thresholds caused by hyperkalaemia.
ecg-tachy-081.aRetenir: Wide-QRS bradycardia in a patient with renal failure = hyperkalaemia: IV calcium first.
ecg-tachy-081.rappel: Treatment of life-threatening hyperkalaemia has three steps. Protect the myocardium: intravenous calcium, whose effect is rapid but transient, repeated if the ECG does not improve. Shift potassium into cells: insulin with glucose, inhaled or intravenous beta-2 agonists, bicarbonate in the presence of acidosis. Remove potassium: dialysis, loop diuretics if urine output is preserved, gastrointestinal binders. Shifting measures do not reduce total body potassium: the level rises again if removal is not ensured, hence close ECG and laboratory monitoring.

ecg-tachy-082.question: Hypokalaemia manifests on the ECG as tall, peaked T waves.
commentaires: Incorrect: tall, peaked T waves are characteristic of hyperkalaemia.
Correct: hypokalaemia flattens the T waves, brings out a U wave, depresses the ST segment and prolongs the QU.
ecg-tachy-082.explication: Tall, peaked T waves are characteristic of hyperkalaemia. Hypokalaemia, by contrast, causes T-wave flattening, a prominent U wave (sometimes larger than the T wave), ST-segment depression and apparent QT (in fact QU) prolongation. In terms of arrhythmias, it predisposes to ectopic beats, AF, VT and above all torsades de pointes, particularly in combination with QT-prolonging drugs or digoxin. Correction of potassium (and magnesium) is part of the treatment of any ventricular arrhythmia.
ecg-tachy-082.aRetenir: Hypokalaemia: flat T waves, U wave, ST depression, long QU, torsades.
ecg-tachy-082.rappel: Hypokalaemia slows repolarisation, particularly phase 3, and increases heterogeneity between myocardial layers; it favours early and delayed afterdepolarisations and enhances digoxin toxicity. It is often associated with hypomagnesaemia (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea), which sustains renal potassium wasting and makes hypokalaemia refractory until magnesium is corrected. ECG signs become clearer as the fall deepens, but their absence does not exclude arrhythmic risk, particularly with QT-prolonging treatment.

ecg-tachy-083.question: In a patient with severe hyperkalaemia, why may a pacemaker or temporary pacing lose capture?
options: It raises the myocardial pacing threshold
It lowers the pacing lead impedance
It prematurely depletes the generator battery
It causes oversensing of P waves
commentaires: Correct: partial depolarisation of the resting membrane reduces excitability; thresholds rise, especially above 7 mmol/l.
Incorrect: pacing impedance is not involved.
Incorrect: the battery is not involved; it is the myocardium that becomes less excitable.
Incorrect: in ICD patients, hyperkalaemia can cause T-wave oversensing, not P-wave oversensing; and this does not explain loss of capture.
ecg-tachy-083.explication: Hyperkalaemia partially depolarises the resting membrane of myocytes and inactivates some of the sodium channels: excitability falls and atrial and ventricular pacing thresholds rise, generally above 7 mmol/l. The atrium is more susceptible than the ventricle to this loss of capture. Very wide paced QRS complexes and prolongation of the interval between the pacing spike and QRS onset (latency) are also seen, which may progress to Wenckebach-type, 2:1 and then complete exit block (ineffective spikes). Pacing impedance and the battery are not involved; in ICD patients, however, hyperkalaemia can cause T-wave oversensing (risk of inappropriate shocks). In practice, when faced with unexplained loss of capture in a patient with renal failure, the first step is to check serum potassium: treating the hyperkalaemia takes priority over reprogramming.
ecg-tachy-083.aRetenir: Hyperkalaemia (especially > 7 mmol/l): rising pacing thresholds, latency, then loss of capture; check serum potassium.
ecg-tachy-083.rappel: The pacing threshold is the minimum energy able to depolarise the myocardium in contact with the electrode; it is described by the strength–duration curve (rheobase, chronaxie). The programmed safety margin must cover its variations. Besides hyperkalaemia, factors raising the threshold include class IC antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide), ischaemia or infarction at the lead site, acidosis, hypoxia and lead maturation. Latency is the delay between the pacing spike and the onset of depolarisation; its prolongation reflects reduced local excitability or conduction and may precede exit block.

ecg-tachy-084.question: What arrhythmic manifestations can severe hyperkalaemia produce?
options: Bradycardia, high-grade AV block or sinoventricular rhythm with no visible P waves
Very wide-QRS sine-wave tachycardia that can mimic VT
Prominent U wave with torsades de pointes
commentaires: Correct: hyperkalaemia slows conduction at every level; P waves may disappear.
Correct: fusion of the QRS and T wave produces a sine-wave pattern that can be mistaken for VT.
Correct: this is the terminal evolution of severe hyperkalaemia.
Incorrect: U waves and torsades belong to hypokalaemia.
Incorrect: Osborn J waves are typical of hypothermia.
ecg-tachy-084.explication: Severe hyperkalaemia slows conduction at every level: loss of P waves (so-called sinoventricular rhythm, in which sinus activity persists without a visible P wave), AV block, extreme bradycardia and marked QRS widening. Fusion of the QRS and T wave produces a sine-wave pattern which, if fast, can be mistaken for VT. It progresses to VF or asystole. U waves and torsades de pointes belong to hypokalaemia, and Osborn J waves are typical of hypothermia. Any unexplained rhythm or conduction disturbance should prompt measurement of serum potassium, and antiarrhythmic treatment for presumed "VT" would be ineffective, or even dangerous, here.
ecg-tachy-084.aRetenir: Severe hyperkalaemia: bradycardias, wide sine-wave QRS mimicking VT, then VF/asystole.
ecg-tachy-084.rappel: Cardiac tissues vary in their sensitivity to potassium: atrial myocardium is the most sensitive, whereas the sinus node and internodal tracts are more resistant. Hence the sinoventricular rhythm: the sinus impulse reaches the ventricles without visible atrial activation. Hyperkalaemia can also cause ST elevation in the right precordial leads mimicking a Brugada pattern or ischaemia, which resolves after correction. In patients with renal failure, associated hypocalcaemia and acidosis modify the picture and potentiate the cardiac toxicity of potassium.
